iqtisad.b: Because reason immediately recognizes the exhaustive division: something either precedes an event, accompanies it, or comes after it. Denying this exhaustive division is denying a self-evident rational principle.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what does someone deny if he rejects a self-evident rational principle?
iqtisad.b: He denies what is immediately and necessarily known by reason (badīhiyyāt al-ʿaql), making rational discussion with him impossible.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī in the Fourth Introduction of al-Iqtiṣād fī al-Iʿtiqād, what is the third source from which the premises of a proof may be established?
iqtisad.b: The third source is mass-transmitted knowledge (tawātur), which produces certain knowledge through widespread, independent transmission that makes collusion upon falsehood impossible.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī use tawātur (mass transmission) to prove the Prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ?
iqtisad.b: He argues: (1) Whoever comes with a miracle is truthful. (2) Muhammad ﷺ came with a miracle, namely the Qur'an. If someone denies that Muhammad ﷺ brought the Qur'an, this is established through tawātur, just as many universally known historical facts are established.

iqtisad.f: Which historical facts does al-Ghazālī cite as examples of knowledge established through tawātur?
iqtisad.b: He mentions knowledge of the existence of Muhammad ﷺ, his claim to Prophethood, the existence of Makkah, and the existence of Mūsā (Moses), ʿĪsā (Jesus), and the other prophets.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the fourth source from which the premises of a proof may be established?
iqtisad.b: The fourth source is a conclusion previously established by another proof. Once something has been demonstrated, it can itself become a premise in a new argument.

iqtisad.f: What example does al-Ghazālī give of using a previously proven conclusion as the premise of a new argument?
iqtisad.b: After proving that the universe is originated, one may use that conclusion as a premise in another syllogism: Every originated thing has a cause. The universe is originated. Therefore, the universe has a cause.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why can a previously demonstrated conclusion serve as a premise in another proof?
iqtisad.b: Because once a proposition has been established with certainty, denying it is no longer reasonable, so it may legitimately function as the basis for further arguments.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the fifth source from which the premises of a proof may be established?
iqtisad.b: The fifth source is revealed evidence (samʿiyyāt), meaning premises accepted on the authority of revelation by someone who already accepts the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī illustrate the use of revealed evidence (samʿiyyāt) in theological reasoning?
iqtisad.b: He argues that all existing things occur by Allah's will. Since sins undeniably exist, they too occur by Allah's will. The universal premise is established by revelation, including the consensus on the statement: "Whatever Allah wills occurs, and whatever He does not will does not occur."

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, who can be compelled by arguments based on revealed evidence (samʿiyyāt)?
iqtisad.b: Only someone who already accepts the authority of revelation or whose acceptance of revelation has already been established through proof.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the sixth source from which the premises of a proof may be established?
iqtisad.b: The sixth source consists of the opponent's own accepted beliefs and assumptions. Even if those beliefs are not independently proven, they may be used against the opponent because he has already committed himself to accepting them.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī allow the use of an opponent's own accepted beliefs as premises in debate?
iqtisad.b: Because once an opponent has accepted a belief, he cannot consistently deny conclusions that necessarily follow from it without contradicting his own position.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, are all six sources of premises equally useful with every audience?
iqtisad.b: No. Their usefulness depends upon the audience. Some sources are universally valid, while others are only persuasive for particular groups.

iqtisad.f: Which sources of premises does al-Ghazālī regard as universally useful for rational discussion?
iqtisad.b: Sense perception and self-evident rational principles are generally useful for everyone who possesses the relevant senses and sound reason.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why are sensory premises not universally available to every individual?
iqtisad.b: Because a sensory premise can only be used by someone who possesses the relevant sense. A blind person cannot use visual observations as premises, and a deaf person cannot use auditory observations.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is tawātur (mass transmission) not universally useful for every person?
iqtisad.b: Because tawātur only benefits someone to whom the reports have actually reached. A person who has never heard the reports cannot yet possess knowledge established by tawātur.

iqtisad.f: What example does al-Ghazālī give to illustrate that tawātur may exist for one group but not another?
iqtisad.b: He notes that certain legal opinions of Imām al-Shāfiʿī were well known among Shāfiʿī jurists but not among ordinary followers, while some of his individual legal rulings were not even widely transmitted among jurists themselves.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, when can a conclusion established by an earlier proof serve as a useful premise?
iqtisad.b: Only for someone who has already understood and accepted the earlier proof establishing that conclusion.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, when are premises based on an opponent's accepted beliefs useful?
iqtisad.b: They are useful only in debate with someone who actually holds those beliefs; they do not independently establish truth for a neutral investigator.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, when are arguments based on revealed evidence useful?
iqtisad.b: They are useful only for someone who already accepts the authority of revelation.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī conclude after discussing the six sources of logical premises?
iqtisad.b: He concludes the introductory material (tamhīdāt) and begins the first major division of the book, which examines the Essence of Allah.

iqtisad.f: What is the first doctrine discussed in al-Ghazālī's section on the Essence of Allah?
iqtisad.b: The first doctrine is the existence of Allah.

iqtisad.f: What is al-Ghazālī's basic proof for the existence of Allah?
iqtisad.b: Premise 1: Every originated thing has a cause. Premise 2: The universe is originated. Conclusion: Therefore, the universe has a cause, namely Allah.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī define "the universe" (al-ʿālam) in his proof for Allah's existence?
iqtisad.b: He defines the universe as everything that exists besides Allah, including all bodies and all their accidents.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, into what four categories can every existent be classified?
iqtisad.b: Every existent is either (1) an indivisible substance (jawhar fard), (2) a body (jism), (3) an accident (ʿaraḍ) existing in a body, or (4) a non-spatial existent that does not exist in a body, namely Allah.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī distinguish between an indivisible substance (jawhar fard) and a body (jism)?
iqtisad.b: An indivisible substance has no composition, whereas a body consists of joined or composite substances.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, how are bodies and accidents known to exist?
iqtisad.b: They are known directly through observation and experience.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to someone who denies the existence of accidents (aʿrāḍ)?
iqtisad.b: He argues that the very act of denying, disputing, speaking, or shouting is itself an accident. Therefore, anyone who disputes the existence of accidents demonstrates their existence by his own actions.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, can Allah be known directly through the senses?
iqtisad.b: No. Allah is not a body, not a spatial substance, and not an accident, so He cannot be perceived through the senses. His existence is known through rational proof rather than sensory perception.

iqtisad.f: In proving that every originated thing has a cause, what objection does al-Ghazālī address first?
iqtisad.b: He first addresses the objection that not every originated thing requires a cause and argues that this principle is self-evidently known by reason once the relevant concepts are properly understood.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī define a "ḥādith" (originated thing) when proving that every originated thing has a cause?
iqtisad.b: A ḥādith is something that was previously nonexistent and then came into existence.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what does he mean by a "cause" (sabab) in the principle "every originated thing has a cause"?
iqtisad.b: He means that which gives preference (murajjiḥ) to existence over nonexistence, bringing a merely possible thing into existence.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that a merely possible thing (mumkin) cannot bring itself into existence?
iqtisad.b: Because its existence is not necessary by its own essence. As long as nothing gives preference to existence over nonexistence, it remains nonexistent. Therefore, an external preferrer is required.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is the principle "every originated thing has a cause" self-evident rather than something requiring proof?
iqtisad.b: Because once the meanings of "originated thing" and "cause" are properly understood, reason necessarily recognizes that something cannot pass from nonexistence to existence without a preferrer that makes its existence actual.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, is the proposition "the universe is originated" self-evident, or does it require proof?
iqtisad.b: It is not self-evident. Unlike the principle that every originated thing has a cause, the claim that the universe is originated must itself be established by demonstration.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, how does he begin proving that the universe is originated?
iqtisad.b: He first limits the discussion to bodies (ajsām) and argues: Every body cannot exist without originated events. Whatever cannot exist without originated events is itself originated. Therefore, every body is originated.

iqtisad.f: What are the two premises al-Ghazālī uses to prove that every body is originated?
iqtisad.b: (1) Every body cannot exist without originated events. (2) Whatever cannot exist without originated events is itself originated. Therefore, every body is originated.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does every body necessarily contain originated events?
iqtisad.b: Because every body is never free from motion or rest, and both motion and rest are originated events.

iqtisad.f: What objection does al-Ghazālī address regarding motion and rest?
iqtisad.b: An opponent may deny either that motion and rest exist as distinct accidents or that they are originated. Al-Ghazālī responds that both their existence and their origination are evident.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does he consider the existence of accidents (aʿrāḍ) to be obvious?
iqtisad.b: Because every rational person directly experiences accidents such as pain, illness, hunger, thirst, and changing conditions within himself, as well as continual changes occurring in external bodies.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does he refuse to spend much time proving the existence of accidents?
iqtisad.b: Because their existence is evident to any sincere seeker. Only an obstinate opponent would deny them, and arguing extensively with such a person is unproductive.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what point do the philosophers themselves concede regarding accidents?
iqtisad.b: They admit that the heavens undergo successive motions and that the four elements continually receive changing forms and accidents. Their disagreement lies elsewhere.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the real point of disagreement between him and the philosophers concerning the origination of the universe?
iqtisad.b: They do not deny that originated accidents continually occur. Rather, they deny the principle that whatever cannot exist without originated events must itself be originated.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, how does the example of the four elements support the existence of originated accidents?
iqtisad.b: The philosophers themselves acknowledge that water changes into air, air into fire, and other elements likewise undergo continual transformations producing minerals, plants, and animals. These changing forms are originated accidents.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is motion necessarily originated?
iqtisad.b: Because every motion begins after previously not existing, and its occurrence is directly observed through experience.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is rest also originated?
iqtisad.b: Because a body that is at rest can begin moving. Once motion occurs, the previous state of rest ceases. Since what is eternal cannot cease to exist, rest must also be originated.

iqtisad.f: What future argument does al-Ghazālī anticipate when proving that rest is originated?
iqtisad.b: He anticipates his later proof that what is eternal cannot cease to exist, using this principle to show that rest, which does cease, cannot be eternal.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī argue that motion is something distinct from the body itself?
iqtisad.b: If motion were identical with the body, then denying motion would amount to denying the body. But one can truthfully say, "This body is not moving," while the body still exists. Therefore, motion is an additional attribute distinct from the body.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī apply the same reasoning to rest?
iqtisad.b: Just as motion is distinct from the body, rest is likewise an attribute distinct from the body itself, since affirming or denying rest does not affirm or deny the body's existence.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what warning does he give about attempting to prove matters that are already obvious?
iqtisad.b: He says that forcing elaborate proofs for self-evident matters often makes them more obscure instead of clearer.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the objection that motion may have been hidden (kumūn) before becoming manifest rather than newly originated?
iqtisad.b: He replies that even if one accepts the theory of hiddenness and manifestation, the body is never free from either the hiddenness or manifestation of motion, and these are themselves originated events. Therefore, his argument remains unaffected.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī decline to refute the theory of hiddenness (kumūn) and manifestation in detail?
iqtisad.b: Because refuting it is unnecessary for the purpose of proving that bodies are never free from originated events, which is all his present argument requires.

iqtisad.f: What objection concerning accidents does al-Ghazālī next consider after discussing hiddenness and manifestation?
iqtisad.b: He considers the claim that accidents do not originate but merely move or transfer from one subject to another.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the claim that accidents can transfer from one subject to another?
iqtisad.b: Because the very concept of an accident makes such transfer impossible once its true nature is properly understood.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why might someone mistakenly think that accidents can transfer between subjects?
iqtisad.b: Because he wrongly compares the relationship of an accident to its subject with the relationship of a body to a place, assuming both kinds of attachment are the same.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the crucial difference between a body's relation to place and an accident's relation to its subject?
iqtisad.b: A body's occupation of a place is an additional relation distinct from the body itself, whereas an accident's existence in its subject is not an additional relation separate from the accident.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what absurd consequence would follow if an accident's attachment to its subject were an additional attribute like a body's attachment to place?
iqtisad.b: The accident would require another accident to establish its attachment, that second accident would require another attachment, and so on without end, resulting in an impossible infinite regress of accidents.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī propose to demonstrate the impossibility of accidents transferring between subjects?
iqtisad.b: By explaining the true nature of accidents and of transfer itself, showing that once these concepts are correctly understood, the impossibility of such transfer becomes evident.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what distinction explains why a body can move from one place while an accident cannot move from one subject?
iqtisad.b: He distinguishes between an accidental attachment and an essential attachment. A body's relation to a place is not essential to its existence, whereas an accident's relation to its subject is essential to the accident itself.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is meant by an "essential" (dhātī) attachment?
iqtisad.b: An essential attachment is one whose removal destroys the thing itself. If the essential attachment ceases, the thing whose essence depends upon it also ceases to exist.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that a body's relation to its place is not essential?
iqtisad.b: Because a body can be conceived independently of any particular place, and the body remains the same even when it moves from one place to another.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī argue that a body's location is distinct from the body itself?
iqtisad.b: We first understand the body itself and only afterwards investigate whether place exists and what its nature is. This shows that occupying a particular place is not part of the body's essence.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī use the example of Zayd's height when explaining accidents?
iqtisad.b: Although height is not literally an accident in his technical terminology, it serves as an accessible illustration of something that cannot be conceived independently of the subject to which it belongs.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why can the height of Zayd not exist independently of Zayd?
iqtisad.b: Because the height is understood only as the height of Zayd. If Zayd were removed, that particular height would also cease to exist.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is an accident's attachment to its subject essential?
iqtisad.b: Because an accident has no independent existence apart from its subject. Its very essence consists in existing in that particular subject.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is the transfer of an accident from one subject to another impossible?
iqtisad.b: Because separating an accident from its subject would destroy the accident itself, since its attachment to that subject is part of its very essence rather than an additional relation.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does moving a body not destroy the body, whereas moving an accident would destroy the accident?
iqtisad.b: A body's relation to place is an additional relation external to its essence, while an accident's relation to its subject is identical with its mode of existence. Removing that relation destroys the accident itself.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what conclusion does he reach regarding the first premise that bodies are never free from originated events?
iqtisad.b: He concludes that bodies are never free from motion or rest, that both are originated, and that they do not transfer from one subject to another. Therefore, bodies are never free from originated events.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what second premise remains to be proven after establishing that bodies are never free from originated events?
iqtisad.b: He still must prove the principle that whatever cannot exist without originated events is itself originated.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī begin proving that whatever cannot exist without originated events must itself be originated?
iqtisad.b: He argues that if the universe were eternal while never free from originated events, then there would necessarily be an infinite series of past originated events, which is impossible.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what general method does he use to prove that an eternal universe is impossible?
iqtisad.b: He employs proof by reductio (reduction to absurdity), arguing that the assumption of an eternal universe leads to impossible consequences.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the first impossibility that follows from the existence of an infinite past?
iqtisad.b: It would require that an actual infinite had already been completed or exhausted, meaning that what has no end had nevertheless come to an end.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī regard the completion of an actual infinite as impossible?
iqtisad.b: Because it is contradictory to claim that something without an end has nevertheless been completed, finished, or brought to its end.

iqtisad.f: What is the second impossibility al-Ghazālī claims follows from an infinite number of past celestial revolutions?
iqtisad.b: An infinite number of revolutions would have to be either even, odd, both even and odd, or neither even nor odd. Since the last two are impossible and the first two also lead to contradictions, the assumption is impossible.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī define an even number in his discussion of the infinite?
iqtisad.b: An even number is one that can be divided into two equal parts, such as ten.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī define an odd number in his discussion of the infinite?
iqtisad.b: An odd number is one that cannot be divided into two equal parts, such as nine.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that an actual infinite cannot meaningfully be classified as even or odd?
iqtisad.b: Because an even number differs from an odd number by one unit. Al-Ghazālī argues that an actual infinite cannot lack or gain a single unit in the way finite numbers can.

iqtisad.f: What is the third impossibility al-Ghazālī claims follows from an infinite number of past celestial revolutions?
iqtisad.b: It would require two infinite totals where one is nevertheless smaller than the other, which he considers impossible.

iqtisad.f: What astronomical example does al-Ghazālī use to argue that one infinite total would be smaller than another?
iqtisad.b: According to the philosophers' astronomy, Saturn completes one revolution every thirty years while the Sun completes one every year. Thus, both would have infinitely many past revolutions, yet Saturn's total would be only one-thirtieth of the Sun's.

iqtisad.f: What second astronomical example does al-Ghazālī use to illustrate unequal infinities?
iqtisad.b: The Moon completes about twelve revolutions per year while the Sun completes one. Thus, both would have infinitely many revolutions, yet the Moon's total would be greater than the Sun's.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does the existence of unequal infinite totals constitute a contradiction?
iqtisad.b: Because something that is genuinely infinite cannot be smaller than another infinite quantity by lacking a finite amount.

iqtisad.f: What objection does al-Ghazālī consider regarding Allah's infinite power and knowledge?
iqtisad.b: An opponent argues that if an infinite past is impossible, then Allah's infinite powers and infinite knowledge should also be impossible.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī distinguish between saying "Allah's powers have no end" and "Allah's knowledge has no end"?
iqtisad.b: When speaking of Allah's power, he refers to a single eternal attribute that never ceases to exist, not to an infinite collection of separate powers.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does saying that Allah's power has no end not imply an actual infinite collection of things?
iqtisad.b: Because it refers to one eternal attribute that remains without ceasing, not to an infinite number of distinct entities.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does he reject the assumption that "Allah's knowledge has no end" means there are infinitely many existing objects?
iqtisad.b: Because the expression is easily misunderstood. It does not necessarily imply an actually infinite collection of existing things, and its proper explanation requires a more detailed discussion than he wishes to give at that point.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what warning does he give about reasoning from the wording of terms alone?
iqtisad.b: He warns that people often assume different expressions have identical meanings simply because the words are grammatically similar, whereas the underlying realities may be entirely different.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what has been established after proving that the universe is originated and that every originated thing has a cause?
iqtisad.b: It has been established that the universe has a cause or maker. However, it has not yet been established whether that cause is itself originated or eternal.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the second major claim concerning Allah's Essence?
iqtisad.b: The second claim is that the Maker of the universe is eternal (qadīm).

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī prove that the Maker of the universe is eternal?
iqtisad.b: He argues that if the Maker were originated, He would require another cause. That cause would require another, leading either to an infinite regress of causes—which is impossible—or to an eternal first cause. Therefore, an eternal first cause must exist.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject an infinite regress of causes?
iqtisad.b: Because an infinite regress could never ultimately explain the existence of originated things. Therefore, the chain of causes must terminate in an eternal first cause.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what does he mean by describing Allah as "eternal" (qadīm)?
iqtisad.b: He means simply that Allah's existence is not preceded by nonexistence.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, is eternity (qidam) an additional attribute distinct from Allah's Essence?
iqtisad.b: No. Eternity is not an additional entity or quality added to Allah's Essence. It simply means that His existence has no prior nonexistence.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject treating eternity (qidam) as a separate attribute requiring another eternity?
iqtisad.b: Because doing so would generate an infinite regress, requiring the eternity itself to possess another eternity, and so on without end.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the third major claim concerning Allah's Essence?
iqtisad.b: The third claim is that Allah is everlasting (bāqī) and can never cease to exist.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī prove that Allah is everlasting?
iqtisad.b: He argues that whatever is eternal cannot cease to exist, because ceasing to exist would itself require a cause, and no possible cause of Allah's nonexistence can exist.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why would the cessation of an eternal being require a cause?
iqtisad.b: Because nonexistence occurring after eternal existence would be a new occurrence, and every new occurrence requires something to bring it about.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why can Allah's nonexistence not be produced by an act of power?
iqtisad.b: Because power produces things that exist, whereas nonexistence is not a thing. Therefore, nonexistence cannot be the direct effect of power.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī argue that producing nonexistence is impossible even if someone claims the nonexistent is "a thing"?
iqtisad.b: He replies that even if someone considers the nonexistent to have an essence, power does not produce that essence; it merely negates its existence, and negation itself is not a thing that can be produced.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why can Allah not cease to exist because of an opposing force or contrary?
iqtisad.b: Because no originated opposite could overcome the Eternal, and no eternal opposite could suddenly begin destroying Him after existing alongside Him eternally.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why can Allah not cease to exist because a necessary condition for His existence disappears?
iqtisad.b: Because any necessary condition would either be originated—which cannot sustain something eternal—or itself eternal, in which case the same argument proving Allah's permanence would also apply to that condition.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, how do accidents (aʿrāḍ) cease to exist?
iqtisad.b: They cease by their own nature. Certain accidents, such as motion, are inherently transient and cannot remain in existence.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say that motion necessarily ceases to exist?
iqtisad.b: Because motion consists in continual renewal. If motion remained unchanged instead of continually ceasing and recurring, it would become rest rather than motion.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is the disappearance of motion different from the impossible disappearance of Allah?
iqtisad.b: Because transience belongs to the very nature of motion, whereas Allah's eternal existence contains no intrinsic tendency toward nonexistence.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why do colors and other accidents cease to exist?
iqtisad.b: They are not eternal by nature, and their continuation is not necessary. Their disappearance does not present the same impossibility that would arise if an eternal being ceased to exist.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, how do substances (jawāhir) cease to exist?
iqtisad.b: They cease when motion and rest are no longer created in them. Without these conditions, their continued existence is impossible.

iqtisad.f: What is the fourth major claim concerning Allah's Essence?
iqtisad.b: The fourth claim is that Allah is not a spatial substance (jawhar) occupying space.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī argue that Allah cannot be a spatial substance?
iqtisad.b: If Allah occupied space, He would necessarily be characterized by motion or rest. Since whatever cannot exist without originated events is itself originated, Allah could not then be eternal.

iqtisad.f: What objection does al-Ghazālī address regarding the use of the term "substance" (jawhar) for Allah?
iqtisad.b: He considers the view of someone who calls Allah a "substance" while denying that He occupies space.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, does reason by itself forbid applying particular names or terms to Allah?
iqtisad.b: No. Reason itself does not prohibit terminology. Restrictions arise from the conventions of language or from revealed law, not from pure reason alone.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what are the two legitimate grounds for rejecting someone's use of a particular term for Allah?
iqtisad.b: A term may be rejected either because it contradicts the established meaning of the language or because it contradicts revealed usage in the Sharīʿah.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, how should someone be judged if he falsely claims that a word literally applies to Allah according to the Arabic language?
iqtisad.b: He is simply mistaken about the language, because he has falsely attributed that literal meaning to the Arabic lexicon.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, when may a metaphorical expression about Allah be acceptable?
iqtisad.b: If the intended resemblance makes the metaphor linguistically appropriate, its use is not objectionable from the standpoint of language.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what if a metaphorical application of a term to Allah is linguistically inappropriate?
iqtisad.b: The speaker has merely misused the language. This is a linguistic error rather than a philosophical or rational one.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does he consider detailed debates about the linguistic appropriateness of particular words to be outside the scope of theology?
iqtisad.b: Because such questions belong to language and rhetoric rather than to rational demonstrations concerning the realities of Allah's nature.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what are the two juristic opinions regarding the permissibility of applying names to Allah that are not explicitly found in revelation?
iqtisad.b: One opinion permits only names explicitly authorized by revelation, making all others impermissible. The other opinion holds that only names explicitly prohibited by revelation are forbidden, unless they mislead people into false beliefs about Allah.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why might a name for Allah be prohibited even if revelation does not explicitly forbid it?
iqtisad.b: Because it may falsely suggest an incorrect belief about Allah's attributes, and creating such false impressions is prohibited.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, does whether a word is misleading depend solely on the word itself?
iqtisad.b: No. Whether a word is misleading depends on the language and customary usage of the people. A word may mislead one community but not another.

iqtisad.f: What is the fifth claim concerning Allah's Essence according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: The fifth claim is that the Maker of the universe is not a body (jism).

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī define a body (jism) in this discussion?
iqtisad.b: A body is something composed of two or more spatially extended substances (jawāhir) occupying space.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that Allah cannot be a body?
iqtisad.b: Because every body is composed of spatial substances, and he has already established that Allah cannot be a spatial substance. Therefore, Allah cannot be a body.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what if someone calls Allah a "body" while intending a different meaning?
iqtisad.b: The dispute concerns language or religious usage, not reason. Pure reason does not determine the permissibility of words themselves.

iqtisad.f: Besides composition, what additional argument does al-Ghazālī give against Allah being a body?
iqtisad.b: Every body has a specific size or dimension. Since it could conceivably be larger or smaller, its particular size would require a determining cause, making it dependent and therefore created rather than the Creator.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that possessing a particular size proves something is created?
iqtisad.b: Because any specific size is one among several possible sizes, and choosing one possibility over another requires a determiner. Whatever requires such a determiner is not self-subsistent.

iqtisad.f: What is the sixth claim concerning Allah's Essence according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: The sixth claim is that the Maker of the universe is not an accident (ʿaraḍ).

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī define an accident (ʿaraḍ) in this discussion?
iqtisad.b: An accident is something whose existence depends upon an underlying subject—namely a body or a spatial substance—in which it inheres.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that Allah cannot be an accident?
iqtisad.b: Because accidents depend on bodies or substances, and those are originated. Since Allah is eternal, He cannot be something dependent upon an originated subject.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what if someone uses the word "accident" to mean a non-spatial divine attribute?
iqtisad.b: He does not deny the existence of such divine attributes. The disagreement concerns terminology, since "Maker" properly refers to the divine Essence possessing the attributes rather than to the attributes themselves.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī illustrate that actions are attributed to the subject rather than its attributes?
iqtisad.b: He compares it to a carpenter: carpentry is attributed to the carpenter himself, not to one of his qualities. Likewise, creation is attributed to Allah's Essence, not to one of His attributes.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, if someone uses the word "accident" with an entirely different meaning, what kind of dispute remains?
iqtisad.b: Only a dispute about language or religious terminology remains, not a dispute about rational truth.

iqtisad.f: What is the seventh claim concerning Allah's Essence according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: The seventh claim is that Allah is not located in any of the six spatial directions.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what are the six spatial directions?
iqtisad.b: Above, below, in front, behind, right, and left.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī define a spatial direction (jihah)?
iqtisad.b: A direction is a place considered in relation to another spatial object. For example, "above" means occupying the place adjacent to another object's upper side.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why are spatial directions meaningful only for bodies and accidents?
iqtisad.b: Because directions presuppose spatial location, and only bodies directly occupy space while accidents relate to space only through the bodies in which they inhere.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what are the two intelligible ways something may be said to occupy a direction?
iqtisad.b: Either it directly occupies space as a substance, or it exists in a body as an accident and therefore occupies direction only by dependence upon that body.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer someone who claims Allah is "in a direction" but intends something other than spatial location?
iqtisad.b: He rejects the wording because it naturally suggests spatial location, but he does not reject the person's intended meaning until it is clearly explained.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say he cannot refute an undefined meaning hidden behind the phrase "Allah is in a direction"?
iqtisad.b: Because one cannot deny a meaning that has not yet been explained. The person must first clarify what he intends.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what harmless meaning might someone intend by saying Allah is "in a direction"?
iqtisad.b: They might simply intend that Allah possesses knowledge and power or another non-spatial attribute, which al-Ghazālī does not reject.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what criterion determines whether an intended meaning behind the phrase "Allah is in a direction" is acceptable?
iqtisad.b: If the intended meaning implies originatedness or created characteristics, it is impossible. If it does not, the wording alone remains objectionable because of its misleading appearance.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that occupying one particular direction would require a determiner?
iqtisad.b: Because all directions are equally possible with respect to something allegedly located in space. Selecting one direction rather than another requires a determining cause.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does requiring a determiner contradict Allah's eternity?
iqtisad.b: Because whatever could have been otherwise is contingent, and contingency requires a determiner. The Eternal, however, exists necessarily and is not contingent in any respect.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the claim that Allah is above because "above" is the noblest direction?
iqtisad.b: He argues that "above" became a meaningful direction only after the creation of the world and living beings. Before creation there was neither "above" nor "below."

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say that "above" and "below" did not exist before creation?
iqtisad.b: Because these directions are defined relative to creatures, such as the head and feet of living beings. Without creation, such relative directions have no meaning.

iqtisad.f: What second argument does al-Ghazālī give against Allah occupying a direction?
iqtisad.b: If Allah were in a direction, He would necessarily stand in spatial relation to the universe as either larger than it, smaller than it, or equal to it.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī consider all three possibilities—larger, smaller, or equal—to be impossible for Allah?
iqtisad.b: Each possibility assigns Allah a measurable size, and any specific size could have been otherwise, requiring a determiner and implying createdness rather than necessary existence.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the objection that if occupying a direction implies having dimensions, then accidents (aʿrāḍ) must also have dimensions?
iqtisad.b: He replies that accidents are not in a direction independently. They occupy direction only through the bodies in which they inhere, so any dimensionality belongs to them only by dependence upon those bodies.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why are accidents considered measurable only by dependence on bodies?
iqtisad.b: Because accidents cannot exist independently. For example, ten accidents require ten substances in which they exist, so their "quantity" follows the quantity of the substances they inhabit.

iqtisad.f: What objection does al-Ghazālī address regarding raising the hands and face toward the sky during supplication?
iqtisad.b: The objection is that if Allah is not literally above, why does Islamic practice and human instinct direct people to raise their hands and faces toward the sky when making duʿāʾ?

iqtisad.f: What objection does al-Ghazālī address concerning the Prophet's ﷺ question to the slave girl, "Where is Allah?"
iqtisad.b: The objection is that the Prophet ﷺ accepted her pointing toward the sky as evidence of her faith, seemingly indicating that Allah is literally above.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī compare the sky being the direction of supplication to the Kaʿbah being the direction of prayer?
iqtisad.b: Just as the Kaʿbah serves as the qiblah for prayer without containing Allah, the sky serves as the symbolic direction of supplication without Allah being located within it.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why did Allah designate the Kaʿbah as the qiblah for prayer?
iqtisad.b: To unite worshippers upon a single direction, which promotes concentration, humility, and presence of heart, while honoring that place by associating it with Himself.

iqtisad.f: Does al-Ghazālī believe Allah is literally present in the Kaʿbah because Muslims face it in prayer?
iqtisad.b: No. Facing the Kaʿbah does not imply that Allah dwells there. It is a divinely designated direction for worship.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, does directing supplication toward the sky imply that Allah resides in the sky?
iqtisad.b: No. The sky is the symbolic direction of duʿāʾ just as the Kaʿbah is the symbolic direction of ṣalāh; neither implies that Allah inhabits those locations.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what spiritual purpose lies behind the bodily act of prostrating on the ground?
iqtisad.b: It trains the heart in humility before Allah by placing the noblest part of the body—the face—upon the lowliest material—the earth—thereby reinforcing inward submission.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does placing one's face upon the earth help cultivate humility?
iqtisad.b: Because the servant remembers that he was created from dust and physically expresses his lowliness before Allah through prostration.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the relationship between bodily actions and the heart?
iqtisad.b: Bodily actions influence and educate the heart, just as bodily actions themselves are guided by the beliefs and states of the heart.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the true place of humility before Allah?
iqtisad.b: True humility belongs to the heart through recognizing one's own lowly status before Allah's majesty, while bodily acts serve to reinforce that inward state.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the heart's role in glorifying Allah compared to the limbs?
iqtisad.b: The heart glorifies Allah by recognizing His supreme rank, while the limbs assist by expressing that reverence through symbolic physical actions.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say the limbs express glorification by pointing upward?
iqtisad.b: Because the highest physical direction naturally symbolizes exalted rank, allowing the body to participate symbolically in the heart's recognition of Allah's transcendence.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, does pointing upward signify Allah's physical location?
iqtisad.b: No. It symbolizes the exaltedness of Allah's rank, not His occupation of a physical place.

iqtisad.f: What linguistic example does al-Ghazālī use to explain symbolic upward direction?
iqtisad.b: People commonly praise someone's high status by saying, "His authority is in the seventh heaven," intending greatness of rank rather than literal physical location.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why do people instinctively point upward when speaking of greatness?
iqtisad.b: Because height naturally serves as a metaphor for superiority, honor, and exalted status rather than literal spatial elevation.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what mistake do people with shallow understanding make regarding gestures toward the sky?
iqtisad.b: They focus only on the outward bodily gesture and assume it proves Allah occupies a location, while overlooking the inward meanings intended for the heart.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the true meaning of Allah's exaltedness (ʿuluww)?
iqtisad.b: Allah's exaltedness refers to the loftiness of His rank, majesty, and perfection—not to physical elevation or location.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what additional reason explains why people naturally face the sky when making duʿāʾ?
iqtisad.b: Supplication seeks Allah's blessings, and revelation describes provisions and divine decrees as descending from the heavens through the angels. Therefore, people instinctively turn toward the symbolic source from which these blessings descend.

iqtisad.f: Which Qur'anic verse does al-Ghazālī cite to explain turning toward the sky during supplication?
iqtisad.b: He cites: "And in the heaven is your provision and that which you are promised." (Qur'an 51:22).

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what role do the angels play in his explanation of facing the sky during supplication?
iqtisad.b: The angels dwell in the heavenly realm and are entrusted with conveying Allah's decrees and provisions, making the heavens a symbolic direction associated with divine blessings.

iqtisad.f: What analogy does al-Ghazālī use to explain why people naturally face the sky when asking Allah for provision?
iqtisad.b: He compares it to people turning toward a king's treasury when provisions are being distributed. They look toward the treasury without believing the king himself resides there.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, does facing the symbolic source of blessings imply that Allah Himself is located there?
iqtisad.b: No. Just as facing a treasury does not mean the king is inside it, facing the heavens does not mean Allah resides there.

iqtisad.f: What overall principle does al-Ghazālī establish regarding bodily gestures in worship?
iqtisad.b: Bodily gestures are symbolic acts that educate and reinforce the heart's inner states of humility, reverence, and hope; they are not proofs that Allah occupies physical space or direction.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why do some ordinary Muslims believe that Allah is in the sky?
iqtisad.b: Because they take the upward gestures used in worship literally and assume that the object of worship is physically located in the heavens. Al-Ghazālī rejects this belief as an error.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain the Prophet's ﷺ acceptance of the slave girl's gesture toward the sky as evidence of her faith?
iqtisad.b: He explains that she was mute, so pointing upward was the only practical way for her to express the exaltedness of Allah and distinguish Him from the idols worshipped on earth.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what was the purpose of asking the slave girl, "Where is Allah?"
iqtisad.b: It was to determine whether she worshipped Allah or earthly idols, not to establish that Allah literally occupies the sky.

iqtisad.f: Why did the slave girl's gesture toward the sky indicate correct belief according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Because it showed that her deity was not one of the idols housed in temples on earth, as the idolaters believed.

iqtisad.f: What objection does al-Ghazālī address regarding denying that Allah occupies a direction?
iqtisad.b: The objection claims that denying direction implies affirming a being that is neither inside nor outside the universe, neither connected to it nor separate from it, which seems impossible.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the claim that every existing thing must be either inside or outside the world?
iqtisad.b: He argues that this applies only to things capable of occupying space or entering spatial relations. A being that is not spatial is not subject to these alternatives.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, when is it impossible for something to be neither connected nor disconnected?
iqtisad.b: Only when the thing is of a kind that can possess connection or separation in the first place.

iqtisad.f: What analogy does al-Ghazālī use to explain why Allah need not be described as either connected or disconnected from the world?
iqtisad.b: He compares it to a stone, which is neither knowledgeable nor ignorant because it lacks the capacity for knowledge altogether. Likewise, Allah is beyond spatial relations because He is not spatial.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why can a stone be neither knowledgeable nor ignorant?
iqtisad.b: Because knowledge and ignorance apply only to living beings. Since a stone lacks the capacity for knowledge, neither description applies to it.

iqtisad.f: What is the necessary condition for something to possess spatial direction or spatial relation according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: It must either occupy space itself or exist within something that occupies space.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is Allah not subject to spatial direction or spatial relations?
iqtisad.b: Because He neither occupies space nor exists within something that occupies space. Therefore, the conditions required for spatial relations are absent.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī argue that a non-spatial being must exist?
iqtisad.b: Since every spatial, originated thing requires a cause, and an infinite regress is impossible, there must exist a cause that is itself not spatial.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what does he say if someone claims that a non-spatial being is "incomprehensible"?
iqtisad.b: He distinguishes between being unimaginable and being unintelligible. Allah is unimaginable to the senses and imagination but fully knowable through rational proof.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what does imagination (khayāl) naturally represent?
iqtisad.b: Imagination represents only things resembling visible bodies that possess shape, size, and color.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say Allah cannot be imagined?
iqtisad.b: Because Allah has neither body, color, shape, nor size, while imagination operates only upon such sensory forms.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the meaning of something being "intelligible" (maʿqūl)?
iqtisad.b: It means that reason is compelled by sound proof to affirm its existence, even if it cannot be imagined.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, does inability to imagine something prove that it does not exist?
iqtisad.b: No. Many real things cannot be pictured by the imagination even though their existence is certain.

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī give of real things that cannot themselves be imagined visually?
iqtisad.b: The imagination itself, sight, knowledge, power, sound, smell, and inner psychological states such as fear, joy, anger, shame, and sorrow.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is imagination an unreliable measure of existence?
iqtisad.b: Because imagination attempts to represent everything as though it were a visible body with shape and color, even when the thing is not bodily by nature.

iqtisad.f: What conclusion does al-Ghazālī draw from the limitations of imagination?
iqtisad.b: The inability to imagine Allah does not undermine His existence, since rational proof establishes realities beyond the reach of imagination.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say he devoted extra discussion to this issue despite aiming for brevity?
iqtisad.b: Because many theological summaries spend too much time on obvious matters while neglecting the genuinely difficult objections that require clarification.

iqtisad.f: What is the eighth claim concerning Allah's Essence according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: The eighth claim is that Allah is not described as sitting upon or being established on the Throne in a bodily manner.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī argue against interpreting Allah's establishment upon the Throne as physical?
iqtisad.b: Anything resting upon a body must itself possess measurable size and dimensions, which would imply createdness. Allah is beyond all bodily measurement.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why would physically touching the Throne be impossible for Allah?
iqtisad.b: Because if Allah could touch the Throne from one side, He could in principle be touched from all sides, making Him surrounded by bodies, which is impossible.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what kinds of things can literally rest upon a body?
iqtisad.b: Only another body can literally rest upon a body, while only an accident can literally inhere in one. Allah is neither a body nor an accident.

iqtisad.f: Which Qur'anic verse does al-Ghazālī discuss regarding Allah's establishment over the Throne?
iqtisad.b: "The Most Merciful rose over the Throne" (al-Raḥmān ʿalā al-ʿArsh istawā).

iqtisad.f: Which hadith does al-Ghazālī discuss concerning Allah's descent?
iqtisad.b: The hadith stating that Allah descends every night to the lowest heaven.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, into which two groups does he divide people when explaining such texts?
iqtisad.b: He divides them into ordinary believers (ʿawāmm) and scholars (ʿulamāʾ).

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, how should ordinary believers be taught regarding verses and hadiths that could suggest anthropomorphism?
iqtisad.b: They should not be drawn into detailed figurative interpretations. Instead, they should firmly believe that Allah is unlike His creation and free from all created characteristics.

iqtisad.f: What foundational belief should ordinary believers hold regarding Allah according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: They should believe that "There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing," while rejecting any resemblance between Allah and creation.

iqtisad.f: How should scholars respond if ordinary believers ask about the detailed meanings of such texts?
iqtisad.b: They should discourage speculative discussion and redirect them, explaining that such specialized matters belong to qualified scholars.

iqtisad.f: Which statement of Imām Mālik does al-Ghazālī cite concerning Allah's istiwāʾ?
iqtisad.b: "The istiwāʾ is known, its modality is unknown, asking about it is an innovation, and believing in it is obligatory."

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, how should scholars (not ordinary people) approach anthropomorphic Qur'anic verses and hadiths about Allah?
iqtisad.b: Scholars should understand and explain their intended meanings. While detailed interpretation is not individually obligatory, scholars should know how to reconcile such texts with Allah's transcendence and avoid attributing corporeal qualities to Him.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, are verses such as "The Most Merciful rose over the Throne" and "Allah descends to the lowest heaven" considered meaningless mutashābih texts?
iqtisad.b: No. Unlike the disconnected letters at the beginning of some sūrahs, these expressions are meaningful Arabic phrases. They convey a correct meaning to scholars, though they may mislead the ignorant if understood literally.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī distinguish anthropomorphic texts from the disconnected letters (ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿāt)?
iqtisad.b: Because the disconnected letters were not originally established in Arabic to signify known meanings, whereas expressions like "descends" and "rose over" are meaningful Arabic words capable of literal and metaphorical usage.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain the verse "He is with you wherever you are" (Qur'an 57:4)?
iqtisad.b: Ordinary people may imagine physical proximity, but scholars understand that "withness" refers to Allah's encompassing knowledge and awareness, not physical location.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what does the hadith "The believer's heart is between two fingers of the Most Merciful" mean?
iqtisad.b: It does not refer to literal fingers of flesh. Rather, "fingers" symbolize Allah's complete power to turn and direct hearts however He wills.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī interpret the word "finger" metaphorically in this hadith?
iqtisad.b: Because the essential purpose of a finger in this context is the ability to manipulate and turn something. The word is therefore used metaphorically to express Allah's absolute power over hearts.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why do Arabic expressions sometimes mention a cause while intending its effect?
iqtisad.b: Arabic commonly uses the cause as a metaphor for its result or effect. Thus words like "finger," "anger," and "pleasure" can refer to what they produce rather than their literal meanings.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī interpret Allah's saying in the hadith qudsī: "Whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running"?
iqtisad.b: Walking and running do not indicate bodily movement. They symbolize the rapid outpouring of Allah's mercy, generosity, and acceptance toward His servant.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī interpret the statement: "The longing of the righteous to meet Me has become long, and My longing to meet them is even greater"?
iqtisad.b: Allah's "longing" is not emotional need or pain. It metaphorically refers to His abundant mercy, favor, and gracious reception of His servants.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī interpret Qur'anic references to Allah's anger and pleasure?
iqtisad.b: They are metaphors for Allah's will to punish or reward, since anger and pleasure are described by their effects rather than as human emotions.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī interpret the statement that the Black Stone is "the right hand of Allah on earth"?
iqtisad.b: It is a metaphor likening the Black Stone to the hand of a king that people kiss in allegiance and honor. It does not imply Allah literally possesses a physical hand located in the Kaʿbah.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what possible relationships can exist between Allah and the Throne when interpreting the verse "The Most Merciful rose over the Throne"?
iqtisad.b: Possible relations include being known, willed, having power over it, being a substrate for it, or being located upon it. Corporeal relations such as occupying a place or serving as a substrate are impossible for Allah.

iqtisad.f: Which relationship between Allah and the Throne does al-Ghazālī conclude is intended by the verse "The Most Merciful rose over the Throne"?
iqtisad.b: He concludes that it refers to Allah's dominion, mastery, and complete power over the Throne—the greatest of created things—rather than physical sitting or location.

iqtisad.f: What linguistic evidence does al-Ghazālī provide for interpreting "istawā" (rose over) as dominion rather than physical sitting?
iqtisad.b: Arabic allows expressions such as "The ruler established authority over Iraq" (istawā ʿalā al-ʿIrāq) to mean gaining control and sovereignty rather than physically sitting upon it.

iqtisad.f: Which poetic example does al-Ghazālī cite to support the metaphorical meaning of "istawā"?
iqtisad.b: He cites the verse: "Bashīr established authority over Iraq without sword or bloodshed" (qad istawā Bashīr ʿalā al-ʿIrāq min ghayri sayfin wa-damin muhrāq), where istawā clearly means dominion rather than physical sitting.

iqtisad.f: Which interpretation of "The Most Merciful rose over the Throne" does al-Ghazālī attribute to some early scholars (salaf)?
iqtisad.b: Some explained it by analogy with the verse "Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke," understanding istawā as directing power and authority rather than bodily sitting.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what are the two main methods of interpreting the hadith "Allah descends to the lowest heaven"?
iqtisad.b: Either the attribution of descent to Allah is metaphorical while the actual descent is that of one of His angels, or the word "descent" itself is interpreted metaphorically.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī justify interpreting Allah's "descent" as the descent of an angel?
iqtisad.b: Arabic commonly attributes the actions of followers or representatives to the one they represent, just as people may say "The king arrived," intending the arrival of his army or entourage.

iqtisad.f: What linguistic example does al-Ghazālī use to illustrate attributing an action to a leader when it is actually performed by his followers?
iqtisad.b: People may say, "The king has arrived at the city gate," meaning that his army has arrived, even if the king himself has not yet reached the city.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the second major interpretation of the hadith "Allah descends to the lowest heaven"?
iqtisad.b: "Descent" may be understood metaphorically as Allah's gracious condescension, mercy, and kindness toward His servants rather than literal movement from one place to another.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, how is the word "descent" used metaphorically in Arabic regarding people?
iqtisad.b: It is used to describe humility, gentleness, and lowering oneself toward others, just as "rising" is used metaphorically for pride, greatness, and exaltation.

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī give of metaphorical "rising" in Arabic?
iqtisad.b: Expressions such as "He raised his head to the sky" (meaning he became arrogant), "He rose to the highest ranks," or "His status is in the seventh heaven" all signify exalted rank rather than physical elevation.

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī give of metaphorical "descending" in Arabic?
iqtisad.b: Expressions such as "He descended to the lowest rank" or "He lowered himself to the ground" refer to humility, gentleness, or loss of status rather than physical movement.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what are the three possible meanings of "descent" when applied to Allah?
iqtisad.b: (1) Literal movement from place to place, (2) a decrease or loss of rank, or (3) gracious condescension through mercy, kindness, and responding to His servants.

iqtisad.f: Which meaning of Allah's "descent" does al-Ghazālī reject as impossible because it requires spatial movement?
iqtisad.b: Literal movement from one place to another, because movement can only occur in something occupying space, whereas Allah is not spatially located.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject interpreting Allah's "descent" as a lowering of His rank?
iqtisad.b: Because Allah is eternal and perfect in majesty and cannot lose or diminish His exalted status.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, which interpretation of Allah's "descent" remains possible after the impossible meanings are excluded?
iqtisad.b: It signifies Allah's mercy, kindness, gracious response to supplication, and treating His servants with generosity despite His absolute independence from them.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why did some scholars relate the hadith of Allah's descent to the verse "Exalted in degrees, Lord of the Throne" (Qur'an 40:15)?
iqtisad.b: They explained that after hearing of Allah's immense majesty, the Companions felt overwhelmed, so the hadith teaches that despite His transcendence, Allah mercifully responds to those who call upon Him.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is Allah's answering the prayers of His servants described as "descent"?
iqtisad.b: Because answering prayers represents a gracious act of mercy that goes beyond what absolute self-sufficiency alone would require, so it is metaphorically described as "descending" toward His servants.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does Allah describe Himself as "descending" rather than using another expression?
iqtisad.b: The expression encourages believers to pray, worship, bow, and prostrate confidently, assuring them that Allah's majesty does not prevent Him from showing mercy and responding to them.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why would contemplation of Allah's majesty alone discourage worship?
iqtisad.b: Awareness of Allah's overwhelming greatness could leave people feeling too insignificant to approach Him, silencing their tongues, stilling their limbs, and preventing them from praying.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why must believers contemplate both Allah's majesty and His mercy together?
iqtisad.b: Because His majesty inspires reverence while His mercy encourages hope, worship, supplication, and confident turning toward Him.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does the hadith specify the "lowest heaven" rather than simply saying Allah descends?
iqtisad.b: The "lowest heaven" symbolizes the lowest degree of descent or nearness, just as expressions such as rising to the Pleiades or falling to the earth symbolize the highest and lowest possible levels.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does the hadith specify that Allah descends "every night"?
iqtisad.b: Because the night is the time of solitude, when distractions disappear, hearts become more sincere, and supplications are more likely to be genuine and accepted.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does he discuss the beatific vision (ru'yat Allāh) while treating Allah's essence?
iqtisad.b: To demonstrate that denying spatial location does not require denying the vision of Allah, and to explain why Allah can be seen without occupying a place.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is Allah visible (ru'yah) according to Ahl al-Sunnah?
iqtisad.b: Because He truly exists. Visibility belongs to His real existence and essence, just as knowability belongs to every real existent.

iqtisad.f: Does al-Ghazālī mean that Allah is actually being seen at all times when he says He is visible?
iqtisad.b: No. He means Allah is visible in principle (potentially), just as water is describable as thirst-quenching even before anyone drinks it.

iqtisad.f: What two questions does al-Ghazālī distinguish when discussing the beatific vision of Allah?
iqtisad.b: (1) Whether seeing Allah is rationally possible, and (2) whether it will actually occur, which is known only through revelation.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does revelation proving that Allah will be seen also prove that seeing Him is rationally possible?
iqtisad.b: Because revelation cannot truthfully affirm something that is intrinsically impossible. Its occurrence necessarily implies its rational possibility.

iqtisad.f: What is al-Ghazālī's first rational argument for the possibility of seeing Allah?
iqtisad.b: Allah is a real existent whose essence can be known. Since vision is simply another mode of perceiving an existent and does not imply change or imperfection in the object seen, every real existent is in principle visible unless another impossibility prevents it.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does knowledge of Allah prove the possibility of seeing Him?
iqtisad.b: Knowledge already relates to Allah without changing Him or implying createdness. Since sight likewise does not alter its object, there is no rational reason to deny vision while affirming knowledge.

iqtisad.f: What objection against the beatific vision does al-Ghazālī introduce at the end of this section?
iqtisad.b: The objection claims that if Allah can be seen, He must occupy a direction relative to the observer, and whatever occupies a direction must be a body or accident—which is impossible.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī initially answer the claim that visibility requires spatial direction?
iqtisad.b: He accepts that Allah cannot occupy a direction but denies the hidden premise that being seen necessarily requires occupying a spatial direction.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what are the two premises used to prove that the world is originated (ḥādith)?
iqtisad.b: The proof consists of two premises: (1) Every body (jism) is never free from originated accidents (ḥawādith). (2) Whatever is never free from originated accidents is itself originated. Therefore, every body is originated.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī mean by "the world" (al-ʿālam) when proving its origination?
iqtisad.b: In this proof, he means all bodies and substances (jawāhir), leaving aside accidents for the moment.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say every body is never free from originated accidents?
iqtisad.b: Because every body is always either in motion or at rest, and both motion and rest are originated accidents.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī regard motion as an originated accident?
iqtisad.b: Motion is directly perceived to begin after not existing, making its origination evident through observation.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī argue that rest is also originated?
iqtisad.b: Since a body can move after being at rest, and movement removes the previous state of rest, rest must itself have begun and therefore be originated.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī prove that motion is distinct from the body itself?
iqtisad.b: If motion were identical with the body, then saying "the body is not moving" would negate the body itself. Since the body remains while motion ceases, motion must be something additional to the body.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī consider elaborate proofs for the existence of accidents unnecessary?
iqtisad.b: Because every rational person directly experiences accidents such as pain, hunger, thirst, and changing conditions, making their existence obvious.

iqtisad.f: Against whom is al-Ghazālī mainly arguing regarding the eternity of the world?
iqtisad.b: He is arguing primarily against the philosophers, who admit continual originated motions and changing forms but deny that the world itself is originated.

iqtisad.f: According to the philosophers as described by al-Ghazālī, what do they admit about the heavenly spheres?
iqtisad.b: They admit that the heavenly spheres are perpetually in motion and that each individual motion is originated, although they claim the succession of motions is eternal.

iqtisad.f: According to the philosophers as described by al-Ghazālī, what do they admit about the four elements?
iqtisad.b: They admit that the forms and accidents of the elements continually change through generation and corruption, although they regard the underlying matter as eternal.

iqtisad.f: What point do the philosophers actually dispute in al-Ghazālī's proof?
iqtisad.b: They dispute the premise that whatever never becomes free from originated accidents must itself be originated.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the theory that accidents merely emerge from hidden existence (kumūn) rather than originate?
iqtisad.b: He says that even if one assumed hiddenness and manifestation, the body would still never be free from originated states, which is sufficient for his proof.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the theory that accidents transfer from one subject to another?
iqtisad.b: Because an accident cannot exist independently of its subject; separating an accident from its subject destroys the accident itself rather than transferring it elsewhere.

iqtisad.f: What is the essential difference between a body's relation to place and an accident's relation to its subject?
iqtisad.b: A body's occupation of a place is not intrinsic to its essence and can change, whereas an accident's existence in its subject is intrinsic to its very essence and cannot be separated from it.

iqtisad.f: Why can a body move from one place to another while an accident cannot transfer between subjects?
iqtisad.b: Because place is external to the essence of a body, whereas an accident has no existence apart from the subject in which it inheres.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say imagining an accident transferring between subjects leads to an absurd infinite regress?
iqtisad.b: Because the relation connecting the accident to its new subject would itself require another relation, leading to an endless chain of relations with no first term.

iqtisad.f: What conclusion does al-Ghazālī draw after proving that bodies never become free from originated accidents?
iqtisad.b: He concludes that the first premise of his proof has been established and proceeds to prove the second premise: whatever never becomes free from originated accidents is itself originated.

iqtisad.f: What is the second major premise in al-Ghazālī's proof for the origination of the world?
iqtisad.b: Whatever never becomes free from originated accidents is itself originated.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī argue against an eternal world that continually experiences originated events?
iqtisad.b: He argues that it would require an infinite series of past originated events that has already been completed, which he considers impossible.

iqtisad.f: What is al-Ghazālī's first argument against an actual infinite past?
iqtisad.b: If the past were actually infinite, an infinite number of events would already have been completed, finished, and traversed, which he considers self-contradictory.

iqtisad.f: What is al-Ghazālī's second argument against an actual infinite series of past events?
iqtisad.b: Every number must be either even or odd, but an actually infinite number cannot consistently be classified as either, which he regards as impossible.

iqtisad.f: What is al-Ghazālī's third argument against an actual infinite series of past events?
iqtisad.b: It would require two infinite series of different sizes—for example, the revolutions of Saturn and those of the Sun—even though one infinite quantity cannot be smaller than another.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī use the motions of Saturn and the Sun to argue against an infinite past?
iqtisad.b: Saturn completes one revolution in about thirty years while the Sun completes thirty in the same period. If both had infinitely many past revolutions, one infinite total would be one-thirtieth of the other, which he considers impossible.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the objection that God's objects of power and knowledge are also infinite?
iqtisad.b: He says "God's power has no limit" means His power never ceases, not that there exists an actually infinite collection of things. Likewise, the discussion of God's knowledge differs from an actual infinite collection of existing entities.

iqtisad.f: After proving the world's origination, what syllogism does al-Ghazālī use to establish the existence of the Creator?
iqtisad.b: Every originated thing requires a cause; the world is originated; therefore the world has a cause.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī say has been established immediately after proving that the world has a cause?
iqtisad.b: Only the existence of a cause has been established; whether that cause is eternal or originated must still be demonstrated.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī prove that the world's cause must be eternal?
iqtisad.b: If the cause were originated, it would require another cause, leading either to an impossible infinite regress or to an eternal first cause.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī mean by calling God "eternal" (qadīm)?
iqtisad.b: He means only that God's existence was never preceded by nonexistence; eternity is not an additional attribute separate from His essence.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī prove that God is everlasting (bāqī)?
iqtisad.b: Because whatever is eternal cannot cease to exist, since cessation would itself require a cause to bring about nonexistence.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī deny that nonexistence can be directly produced by divine power?
iqtisad.b: Because power acts upon existent things, whereas nonexistence is not a thing that can be produced as an effect.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain the cessation of accidents?
iqtisad.b: Some accidents, such as motion, are by nature continually renewed and cease immediately after existing; their essence includes continual disappearance.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain the annihilation of substances?
iqtisad.b: Substances cease when God no longer creates the accidents, such as motion and rest, upon which their continued existence depends.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is the beatific vision (ruʾyah) not experienced in this worldly life?
iqtisad.b: Because the soul is occupied by the body and clouded by worldly distractions, which act as veils preventing the highest degree of perception.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī compare the soul's inability to experience the beatific vision in this life?
iqtisad.b: He compares it to physical obstacles such as eyelids, veils, or defects in the eye that prevent ordinary sight despite sight itself being possible.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what will happen to the soul in the Hereafter that enables the beatific vision?
iqtisad.b: After the Resurrection, the soul will be purified, its veils removed, and its perception perfected, allowing a higher degree of knowledge of God than is possible in this world.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī describe the beatific vision in relation to ordinary knowledge?
iqtisad.b: He describes it as a perfection and completion of knowledge, just as ordinary sight is a perfection beyond mere imagination or mental representation.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say expressions such as "seeing God," "beholding God," and "meeting God" are all acceptable?
iqtisad.b: Because once the underlying reality is understood, differences in terminology are unimportant; all refer to the perfected perception granted in the Hereafter.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say it is linguistically appropriate to call this perfected perception "vision" (ruʾyah)?
iqtisad.b: Because if God creates this higher mode of perception in the faculty of sight, calling it "vision" accords most naturally with the ordinary usage of the Arabic language.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what does reason conclude about the possibility of seeing God?
iqtisad.b: Reason not only considers it possible but also recognizes that the human soul naturally longs for such a perfected mode of perception.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī say removes every remaining objection to the beatific vision?
iqtisad.b: Once reason establishes its possibility and revelation affirms its occurrence, any remaining objection arises only from obstinacy, verbal disputes, or failure to understand the concept.

iqtisad.f: Besides rational proof, what type of evidence does al-Ghazālī present for the beatific vision?
iqtisad.b: He presents numerous scriptural proofs, supported by the understanding and consensus of the early Muslims.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī use the prayers of the early Muslims as evidence for the beatific vision?
iqtisad.b: Their repeated supplications asking God for the joy of beholding His Noble Face show that they believed such a vision was possible and expected in the Hereafter.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī consider Prophet Moses عليه السلام' request, "My Lord, show Yourself to me that I may look upon You," to be one of the strongest proofs for the beatific vision?
