iqtisad.b: Because it is impossible that a prophet who spoke directly with God would ask for something that is intrinsically impossible or contradicts God's nature.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what dilemma does Moses عليه السلام' request create for those who deny the beatific vision?
iqtisad.b: They must either accuse Moses عليه السلام of believing false doctrines about God or accuse him of ignorance concerning what they themselves claim is an obvious impossibility.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the claim that Moses عليه السلام believed God was a body located in a direction?
iqtisad.b: Because attributing such ignorance to a prophet amounts to a grave accusation and contradicts the status of the prophets as guides to the truth.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what conclusion should be drawn from Moses عليه السلام' request to see God?
iqtisad.b: The request demonstrates that seeing God is possible in itself, even if it was not granted to Moses عليه السلام during his earthly life.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the objection that Moses عليه السلام asked to see God in this world rather than the Hereafter?
iqtisad.b: He says Moses عليه السلام merely requested something that was possible in itself without knowing whether God had decreed it for that time, just as prophets do not know every unseen matter unless informed by revelation.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī interpret God's reply, "You shall not see Me" (lan tarānī)?
iqtisad.b: He interprets it as a denial of Moses عليه السلام' request in that specific worldly circumstance, not as proof that seeing God is absolutely impossible.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that "You shall not see Me" does not prove the impossibility of seeing God?
iqtisad.b: Because it answers Moses عليه السلام' request concerning the present situation rather than making a universal statement about all times and circumstances.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī interpret the verse, "Vision does not encompass Him" (lā tudrikuhu al-abṣār)?
iqtisad.b: He explains that it means vision cannot fully encompass or surround God, or that it refers specifically to this worldly life rather than denying all vision absolutely.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what mistake do the Ḥashwiyyah make regarding the divine vision?
iqtisad.b: They affirm that God must be in a direction in order to be seen, which leads them to anthropomorphism by attributing bodily characteristics to God.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what mistake do the Muʿtazilah make regarding the divine vision?
iqtisad.b: They correctly deny that God occupies a direction but incorrectly conclude that denying direction requires denying the beatific vision, thereby rejecting clear scriptural evidence.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī characterize the position of Ahl al-Sunnah regarding the beatific vision?
iqtisad.b: Ahl al-Sunnah deny that God is confined to a direction while affirming that He will be seen in the Hereafter, since vision is a perfection of knowledge rather than a consequence of bodily location.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say denying God's direction does not require denying the beatific vision?
iqtisad.b: Because direction is a consequence of corporeality, whereas vision is related to knowledge and does not require the object seen to possess bodily dimensions or location.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī compare vision to knowledge?
iqtisad.b: Both are modes of perception that relate to their object without changing its essence; vision is simply a more complete form of disclosure than ordinary knowledge.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī call the Sunni position "the middle path" (al-iqtiṣād)?
iqtisad.b: Because it avoids the anthropomorphism of the Ḥashwiyyah while also avoiding the excessive negation of the Muʿtazilah, affirming both divine transcendence and the scriptural promise of the beatific vision.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī place the discussion of God's oneness (waḥdāniyyah) within the section on God's essence?
iqtisad.b: Because God's oneness concerns the affirmation of His unique essence and the negation of any equal or partner, rather than an additional attribute distinct from His essence.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, in what first sense is God described as "One" (wāḥid)?
iqtisad.b: God is One in the sense that He has no quantity, magnitude, or parts and therefore cannot be divided.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say God cannot be divided into parts?
iqtisad.b: Because division applies only to things possessing quantity or extension, whereas God has neither quantity nor spatial magnitude.

iqtisad.f: In what second sense does al-Ghazālī describe God as "One"?
iqtisad.b: God is One in the sense that He has no equal, peer (nidd), or rival in His rank and perfection.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī illustrate the meaning of uniqueness without equal?
iqtisad.b: He notes that people say "the sun is one," meaning it has no equal of its kind or rank, not merely that it is numerically one.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say God has no opposite (ḍidd)?
iqtisad.b: Because opposites exist by succeeding one another in the same subject, whereas God does not inhere in any subject and therefore cannot have an opposite.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī mean when he says God has no peer (nidd)?
iqtisad.b: He means that no other being shares God's status as the sole Creator of everything besides Himself.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what three possibilities exist if one supposes God has a partner?
iqtisad.b: The supposed partner would have to be (1) exactly equal to God, (2) greater than God, or (3) inferior to God. All three possibilities are impossible.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the possibility of two beings being completely identical in every respect?
iqtisad.b: Because two things must differ in some respect. Without any distinction, plurality is unintelligible and only one being remains.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain that two identical objects must still differ somehow?
iqtisad.b: If they share the same essence, they must differ by location or time; otherwise there is no basis for distinguishing one from the other.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say two perfectly identical divine beings are impossible?
iqtisad.b: Since God is beyond place and time, no distinction between two identical divine beings could exist; without distinction, multiplicity disappears and only unity remains.

iqtisad.f: Why is it impossible, according to al-Ghazālī, for a partner to be greater than God?
iqtisad.b: Because the greatest and most perfect being alone deserves the title "God"; anything greater would alone be God, making the other not truly divine.

iqtisad.f: Why is it impossible, according to al-Ghazālī, for a partner to be less perfect than God?
iqtisad.b: Because an inferior being lacks the absolute perfection required of divinity and therefore cannot truly be called God in the unrestricted sense.

iqtisad.f: What objection does al-Ghazālī consider regarding multiple creators?
iqtisad.b: Someone might concede that there is only one supreme God but claim that different creators independently created different parts of the universe.

iqtisad.f: What examples of divided creation does al-Ghazālī consider?
iqtisad.b: He considers claims such as one creator making the heavens while another makes the earth, one creating plants while another creates animals, or one creating good while another creates evil.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, into what two general possibilities can all theories of multiple creators be reduced?
iqtisad.b: Either the creators divide the same kinds of created things between themselves, or one creator is responsible for one category of beings while another is responsible for a different category.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the idea that one creator made some bodies while another made different bodies?
iqtisad.b: If both possess equal creative power, each should be capable of creating every body, making the division arbitrary. If one lacks the power to create certain bodies, then that being is imperfect and not truly omnipotent.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī argue that the ability to create one body implies the ability to create all similar bodies?
iqtisad.b: Because bodies share the same essential nature, and an eternal divine power is not restricted to only one member of a class of identical entities.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī conclude that an omnipotent creator cannot be limited to creating only certain bodies?
iqtisad.b: Since bodies are essentially alike, restricting omnipotence to some bodies rather than others would be arbitrary and incompatible with perfect divine power.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the theory that one creator makes substances while another makes accidents?
iqtisad.b: Because accidents cannot exist without substances, and substances likewise require accidents, making the work of each creator dependent upon the other.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what problem arises if one creator depends on another to complete creation?
iqtisad.b: Each creator's action would require the cooperation of the other, meaning either could be prevented from acting and would therefore be incapable of independent creation.

iqtisad.f: Why does mutual dependence disqualify multiple creators from being truly divine according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: A being whose creative activity depends upon another can be obstructed or rendered incapable, whereas true divinity requires absolute independence and unrestricted power.

iqtisad.f: What contradiction would arise if two creators disagreed over creating a substance and its accidents?
iqtisad.b: Each creator's action would obstruct the other's, resulting in mutual prevention (tamānuʿ), which is incompatible with perfect omnipotence.

iqtisad.f: What overall conclusion does al-Ghazālī draw from these arguments about multiple creators?
iqtisad.b: The existence of multiple independent creators is impossible; therefore, the Creator of the universe must be absolutely one without partner or equal.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is a higher degree of knowledge of Allah beyond ordinary intellectual knowledge not impossible?
iqtisad.b: Al-Ghazālī argues that nothing in reason renders such a higher degree of unveiling impossible. Rather, reason affirms its possibility, and human nature itself longs for this greater perfection of knowledge.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why do human beings not attain the highest degree of knowledge of Allah in this worldly life?
iqtisad.b: Because the soul is occupied with the body and clouded by its impurities and worldly distractions, which veil it from attaining this higher degree of perception.

iqtisad.f: What analogy does al-Ghazālī use to explain why the soul is prevented from perceiving higher intelligible realities?
iqtisad.b: He compares it to physical sight: just as an eyelid, a veil, or a defect in the eye can prevent seeing visible objects, the impurities of the soul and worldly preoccupations prevent the perception of higher intelligible realities.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, when will the soul become capable of attaining the highest degree of knowledge and unveiling of Allah?
iqtisad.b: After the Resurrection, when what is hidden is revealed, hearts are purified by the "Pure Drink," cleansed from all impurities, and freed from worldly veils.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī compare the perfected perception of Allah in the Hereafter to ordinary knowledge in this life?
iqtisad.b: He says its superiority over ordinary knowledge is like the superiority of actual sight over mere imagination.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what expressions may be used to describe this perfected perception of Allah in the Hereafter?
iqtisad.b: It may be described as meeting Allah, witnessing Him, seeing Him, beholding Him, or similar expressions, since the wording is secondary once the intended meaning is understood.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why would the term "vision (ru'yah)" be literally correct if this perfected perception were created in the eye?
iqtisad.b: Because if Allah creates this perfected mode of perception in the eye, then the linguistic definition of vision is fulfilled, and there is nothing rationally impossible about such a creation.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is creating this perfected perception in the eye not rationally impossible?
iqtisad.b: Because creating such a perception in the eye is no more impossible than creating it in the heart; both are within Allah's power.

iqtisad.f: What conclusion does al-Ghazālī draw after explaining what Ahl al-Sunnah mean by the vision of Allah?
iqtisad.b: He concludes that reason does not deny this doctrine but rather affirms its possibility, while revelation confirms that it will actually occur.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what objections remain after the doctrine of the vision of Allah is correctly understood?
iqtisad.b: Only obstinate denial, disputes over terminology, or an inability to comprehend the subtle meanings involved.

iqtisad.f: What are the two aspects of al-Ghazālī's discussion of the vision of Allah?
iqtisad.b: The first is demonstrating its rational possibility, and the second is proving its actual occurrence through revelation.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what evidence from revelation strongly supports the occurrence of the vision of Allah in the Hereafter?
iqtisad.b: He says the evidences are so numerous that they amount to consensus, including the believers' repeated supplications asking Allah for the delight of gazing upon His Noble Face and the Prophet's ﷺ explicit statements encouraging that hope.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī consider the believers' supplications for the vision of Allah to be significant evidence?
iqtisad.b: Because the early Muslims unanimously prayed for the delight of seeing Allah, demonstrating that they understood such a vision to be both possible and expected.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī regard Prophet Mūsā's request, "My Lord, show Yourself to me that I may look upon You," as one of the strongest proofs for the possibility of seeing Allah?
iqtisad.b: Because it is inconceivable that a prophet who spoke directly with Allah would ask for something intrinsically impossible or be ignorant of Allah's essential attributes.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what unacceptable implications follow if one claims that Mūsā asked to see Allah despite knowing such a vision was impossible?
iqtisad.b: It would either accuse Mūsā of believing Allah to be a body located in a direction, or accuse him of ignorance regarding Allah's attributes—both of which are unacceptable.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the objection that Mūsā's request to see Allah was made in this world?
iqtisad.b: He replies that Mūsā merely asked for something that is possible in itself without knowing whether Allah had decreed it to occur in this life, just as prophets may pray for matters whose timing has not been revealed to them.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī interpret Allah's statement, "You shall not see Me (lan tarānī)"?
iqtisad.b: He interprets it as a denial of Mūsā's request in that specific worldly circumstance, not as proof that seeing Allah is intrinsically impossible or impossible in the Hereafter.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī interpret the verse, "Vision does not encompass Him (lā tudrikuhu al-abṣār)"?
iqtisad.b: He explains that it means vision cannot completely encompass or surround Allah as it encompasses bodies, or that it refers specifically to this worldly life, not to the Hereafter.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī characterize the positions of the Hashwiyyah, the Muʿtazilah, and Ahl al-Sunnah regarding Allah's vision?
iqtisad.b: He says the Hashwiyyah affirmed direction and thus fell into anthropomorphism, the Muʿtazilah denied the vision because they denied direction, while Ahl al-Sunnah denied direction yet affirmed the vision because vision is related to knowledge rather than corporeality.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does Ahl al-Sunnah affirm the vision of Allah while denying that Allah is in a direction?
iqtisad.b: Because direction follows from corporeality and is therefore denied, whereas vision is a perfection related to knowledge and does not require corporeality or spatial direction.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that Allah's ability to create one substance or accident implies His ability to create others like it?
iqtisad.b: Because the ability to produce one thing necessarily includes the ability to produce its like. Since Allah creates substances and accidents, it is impossible that He be unable to create similar substances and accidents indefinitely.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is Allah's power not limited to a fixed number of possible things?
iqtisad.b: Because possibility itself is not limited to any finite number, and the nature of divine power does not distinguish between one possible object and another. Therefore, His power extends to every possible thing.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain that Allah's power relates equally to all possible motions, colors, and substances?
iqtisad.b: Since His power has already related to motions, colors, and substances of every kind, there is no rational basis for excluding any similar possible motion, color, or substance from the scope of His power.

iqtisad.f: What general principle does al-Ghazālī use to prove that Allah's power encompasses every possible thing?
iqtisad.b: Whatever necessarily belongs to one thing also belongs to everything exactly like it. Since Allah's power relates to some possible things, it must relate to all things sharing the same possibility.

iqtisad.f: What is the first subsidiary issue (farʿ) that al-Ghazālī discusses after proving the universality of Allah's power?
iqtisad.b: He examines whether the opposite of what Allah eternally knows (khilāf al-maʿlūm) is within Allah's power.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what must be understood before determining whether the opposite of Allah's eternal knowledge is within His power?
iqtisad.b: One must first understand the precise meanings of "possible (mumkin)" and "impossible (muḥāl)," because confusion over these terms causes the disagreement.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say careless use of the terms "possible" and "impossible" leads to contradiction?
iqtisad.b: Because without distinguishing different respects of consideration, one may wrongly describe the same thing as both possible and impossible, thereby affirming contradictory statements.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, in what three different respects may the existence of the world be described as necessary, impossible, and possible?
iqtisad.b: It is necessary when considered together with Allah's eternal will to create it; impossible when considered together with the absence of that will; and possible when considered solely in itself without regard to the divine will.

iqtisad.f: Why is the world's existence necessary when considered together with Allah's eternal will?
iqtisad.b: Because once Allah's eternal will to create the world is assumed, the existence of its object necessarily follows, and its nonexistence becomes impossible.

iqtisad.f: Why is the world's existence impossible when considered together with the absence of Allah's will to create it?
iqtisad.b: Because its existence without Allah's will would require an effect without a cause, which is impossible.

iqtisad.f: Why is the world's existence considered possible when regarded only in itself?
iqtisad.b: Because when one considers only the world's essence without reference to Allah's will or any external cause, its nature is merely possible rather than necessary or impossible.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, how can one and the same thing be both possible and impossible without contradiction?
iqtisad.b: It is possible with respect to its own essence but impossible because of something external to it. Contradiction would arise only if it were both possible and impossible in exactly the same respect.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, how does this distinction apply to Allah's eternal knowledge that Zayd will die on Saturday morning?
iqtisad.b: Zayd's being alive at that time is possible in itself, but impossible because it would contradict Allah's eternal knowledge, whose contradiction is impossible.

iqtisad.f: In what sense does al-Ghazālī maintain that Zayd's life at a time contrary to Allah's eternal knowledge remains within Allah's power?
iqtisad.b: Because life, considered simply as life, is itself possible, and Allah's power is fully capable of creating it. Its impossibility arises only from its conflict with Allah's eternal knowledge, not from the nature of life itself.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the claim that Allah's power is deficient with respect to creating something contrary to His eternal knowledge?
iqtisad.b: Because the impossibility lies not in any weakness or limitation of divine power but in the impossibility of Allah's eternal knowledge becoming false.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what does an opponent mean by saying that something contrary to Allah's eternal knowledge is "not within Allah's power"?
iqtisad.b: The opponent means that its existence would entail an impossibility, namely the falsification of Allah's eternal knowledge. Al-Ghazālī accepts this meaning but denies that it justifies denying divine power in the proper sense.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī conclude that it is linguistically correct to say that Allah has power over something contrary to His eternal knowledge?
iqtisad.b: Because ordinary language describes a person as having power over opposite actions, even though Allah eternally knows which action will occur. This usage supports saying that the act remains within the scope of power.

iqtisad.f: What is the second subsidiary issue (farʿ) that al-Ghazālī raises concerning the universality of Allah's power?
iqtisad.b: He considers whether the voluntary actions of humans and other living creatures are also within Allah's power.

iqtisad.f: Why would denying that the actions of living creatures are within Allah's power undermine al-Ghazālī's doctrine?
iqtisad.b: Because it would contradict his principle that Allah's power extends universally to every possible thing.

iqtisad.f: What apparent difficulty arises if the actions of living creatures are said to be within both Allah's power and the creature's power?
iqtisad.b: It appears to imply that a single act is simultaneously under the power of two different agents, which opponents claim is impossible.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the denial that humans and other living creatures possess power?
iqtisad.b: Because human power is known by necessity and affirmed by revelation, since divine commands and obligations would be meaningless if people possessed no power whatsoever.

iqtisad.f: What are the three major positions regarding human power and divine power that al-Ghazālī discusses?
iqtisad.b: He discusses the positions of the Jabriyyah (Compulsionists), the Muʿtazilah, and Ahl al-Sunnah.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the Jabriyyah's position regarding human power?
iqtisad.b: They deny that human beings possess any real power over their voluntary actions.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what consequence follows from the Jabriyyah's denial of human power?
iqtisad.b: It requires denying the self-evident distinction between involuntary movements, such as trembling, and voluntary movements performed by choice.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that the Jabriyyah's doctrine makes the obligations of the Sharīʿah impossible?
iqtisad.b: Because legal responsibility and divine commands become meaningless if human beings possess no power to perform or refrain from actions.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the Muʿtazilah's position regarding Allah's power over the actions of created beings?
iqtisad.b: They deny that Allah's power relates to the voluntary actions of humans, angels, jinn, devils, and animals, claiming that these actions are created solely by the creatures themselves.

iqtisad.f: What first serious error does al-Ghazālī attribute to the Muʿtazilah's doctrine concerning human actions?
iqtisad.b: It contradicts the unanimous belief of the early Muslims that there is no creator or originator besides Allah.

iqtisad.f: What second serious error does al-Ghazālī attribute to the Muʿtazilah's doctrine concerning human actions?
iqtisad.b: It attributes creation and origination to creatures who are themselves ignorant of the detailed actions they supposedly create.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī use ordinary human actions to argue against the Muʿtazilah?
iqtisad.b: He argues that people do not even know the number, details, or precise characteristics of their own movements, making it unreasonable to claim that they independently create them.

iqtisad.f: What example of an infant does al-Ghazālī use to show that complex voluntary actions occur without detailed knowledge?
iqtisad.b: A newborn instinctively crawls toward its mother's breast and suckles despite possessing no knowledge of the complex actions involved.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī use the example of a kitten to argue against attributing independent creation to creatures?
iqtisad.b: A newborn kitten, while its eyes are still closed, instinctively crawls to its mother's milk without possessing knowledge of how to perform such actions.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī use the spider's web as evidence against the Muʿtazilah?
iqtisad.b: A spider weaves geometrically remarkable webs whose symmetry astonishes skilled engineers, despite the spider having no knowledge of geometry.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why do bees build their honeycombs in the shape of hexagons rather than squares, circles, or other polygons?
iqtisad.b: Because the hexagon uniquely combines efficient packing with maximum capacity, minimizing wasted space while closely approximating a circular shape.

iqtisad.f: What geometric principle does al-Ghazālī mention regarding circles and packing?
iqtisad.b: Circular shapes always leave empty gaps when packed together tightly.

iqtisad.f: Why are squares less suitable than hexagons for honeycombs, according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Although squares fit together without gaps, they enclose circular bodies less efficiently because their corners lie far from their centers.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, do bees understand the geometric principles behind hexagonal honeycombs?
iqtisad.b: No. Rather, Allah directs and compels them toward this design without their understanding its mathematical wisdom.

iqtisad.f: What conclusion does al-Ghazālī draw from the remarkable skills displayed by animals?
iqtisad.b: These wonders demonstrate Allah's greatness and creative power, not the independent creative ability of the animals themselves.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī criticize those who believe creatures independently create their own actions?
iqtisad.b: He says they are deceived by their weak and limited abilities into imagining that they share with Allah in creation and origination, whereas Allah alone possesses true dominion and creative power.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what middle path does Ahl al-Sunnah adopt between the Jabriyyah and the Muʿtazilah?
iqtisad.b: Ahl al-Sunnah rejects both absolute compulsion and independent human creation, affirming instead that one action can be related to two powers in different respects.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is it not impossible for one action to be attributed to two powers?
iqtisad.b: Because the two powers relate to the action in different ways. The impossibility would arise only if they related to it in exactly the same respect.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī believe Ahl al-Sunnah must affirm two powers with respect to one voluntary action?
iqtisad.b: Because reason proves that voluntary motion differs from involuntary trembling by human power, while other proofs establish that every possible created event falls under Allah's power.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī distinguish voluntary movement from involuntary trembling?
iqtisad.b: Even if a person desires the trembling to stop, trembling differs from voluntary movement by the presence of human power and choice in the latter.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that a servant's voluntary act must also fall under Allah's power?
iqtisad.b: Because every created event is possible, and every possible thing necessarily falls within the scope of Allah's universal power.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the idea that Allah's power applies to involuntary movements but not to voluntary ones?
iqtisad.b: Because both are equally created events and equally possible. Since voluntary motion is no different from involuntary motion in this respect, Allah's power must encompass both alike.

iqtisad.f: What impossible consequence does al-Ghazālī say follows if Allah's power did not extend to voluntary human actions?
iqtisad.b: If Allah wished to keep a servant's hand still while the servant wished to move it, impossible contradictions concerning movement and rest would result, undermining the concept of power itself.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the claim that Allah's power simply overrides the servant's power because it is stronger?
iqtisad.b: Because both powers relate to the same act in terms of origination, and the relation of one power to that particular act is not inherently stronger than the relation of the other.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what conclusion follows from combining the proof of human power with the proof of Allah's universal power?
iqtisad.b: It necessarily follows that one and the same voluntary action is related to two agents through two distinct kinds of power.

iqtisad.f: What objection does al-Ghazālī next address after concluding that one action is related to two powers?
iqtisad.b: He addresses the objection that such a doctrine is unintelligible and that a single action belonging to two agents cannot be understood.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī mean by God's creation of human actions while humans still possess power?
iqtisad.b: Al-Ghazālī explains that God creates both the human's power and the action itself. Thus God alone is the Creator and Originator of the action, while the human truly possesses power over the action, distinguishing voluntary acts from involuntary ones like trembling.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say God alone is called the Creator (Khāliq) and Originator (Mukhtariʿ)?
iqtisad.b: Because both the created power and the created action exist solely by God's eternal power. Since He brings both into existence, He alone deserves the names Creator and Originator.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī deny that humans are creators of their actions?
iqtisad.b: Although humans possess power when they act, the action is not brought into existence by their power. Rather, God creates both the power and the action, so humans are not creators or originators in the true sense.

iqtisad.f: What term does al-Ghazālī use for the human's relation to actions if it is not creation?
iqtisad.b: He calls it kasb (acquisition), following the Qur'anic terminology for human deeds, while distinguishing it from divine creation.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī prefer the term kasb over khalq (creation)?
iqtisad.b: Because khalq properly belongs only to God, who creates both power and action. Human involvement requires a different term, so he adopts kasb from the Qur'an.

iqtisad.f: What objection does al-Ghazālī address regarding created human power?
iqtisad.b: The objection claims that if created power does not affect the action, it is meaningless, since power without a corresponding object would be like knowledge without something known.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the claim that power must produce its object?
iqtisad.b: He argues that this assumption is false because not every relation (taʿalluq) requires production. Just as knowledge and will relate to their objects without producing them, power can also possess a kind of relation that does not itself create the action.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī use pre-action power to refute his opponents?
iqtisad.b: He notes that even according to his opponents, human power exists before the action occurs. Since the action does not yet exist, power must already have a relation to its object without yet producing it. Therefore, relation is broader than actual production.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what kind of relation does power have before an action occurs?
iqtisad.b: It possesses a genuine relation to the future action even before the action exists. This demonstrates that the relation of power is not limited to bringing the action into existence.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the claim that pre-action power merely "awaits" future relation?
iqtisad.b: Because that would mean the attribute of power presently has no relation at all, only a future one, making it cease to be a relational attribute until the action occurs, which he considers impossible.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the claim that power is merely "prepared" to produce the action?
iqtisad.b: He argues that saying power is merely "prepared" simply postpones the problem, since preparedness itself does not explain an actual present relation between power and its object.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī distinguish his doctrine from that of his opponents regarding power?
iqtisad.b: Both affirm an existing power related to an action before the action occurs. The difference is that al-Ghazālī says the action is ultimately brought into existence by God's power, not by the created human power.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī believe the existence of God's creative power does not negate human power?
iqtisad.b: Because the human power remains genuinely related to the action even though the action is actually created by God's power. The existence of God's creative act does not destroy the created relation possessed by the human.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the claim that power which does not create is identical to incapacity?
iqtisad.b: He distinguishes experiential reality from metaphysical causation. Humans directly perceive the difference between voluntary ability and helplessness, even if their power does not independently create the action.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject equating human power with helplessness?
iqtisad.b: Because this contradicts immediate experience. A person clearly distinguishes voluntary movement from involuntary trembling, showing that power is experientially different from incapacity.

iqtisad.f: In what limited sense does al-Ghazālī admit human power resembles incapacity?
iqtisad.b: Only when compared to God's unlimited power. Relative to divine omnipotence, created power appears deficient, but this does not make it true incapacity.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say attributing limitation to creatures is more appropriate than attributing it to God?
iqtisad.b: Since creatures are inherently finite and dependent, any deficiency belongs to them rather than to God, whose power is perfect and unrestricted.

iqtisad.f: What is the third subsidiary issue (farʿ) discussed after God's universal power?
iqtisad.b: Whether generated effects (mutawallidāt), such as the movement of a ring caused by a moving hand or water moved by the hand, are also directly created by God.

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī's opponent give of generated effects (mutawallidāt)?
iqtisad.b: The movement of a ring caused by the movement of the hand and the movement of water caused by a hand moving through it.

iqtisad.f: Why do opponents argue that generated effects are not directly created by God?
iqtisad.b: Because such effects necessarily follow preceding motions. They argue that if God created each independently, He could create the hand's motion without the ring's motion, which they consider impossible.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī initially respond to the argument from generated effects?
iqtisad.b: He first states that a doctrine must be properly understood before it can be accepted or rejected. Without first clarifying the meaning of the claim, debate over it is premature.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī define tawallud (generation) in its ordinary linguistic sense?
iqtisad.b: He says tawallud ordinarily means that one body emerges from within another body, such as a child emerging from its mother's womb or a plant emerging from the earth.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject applying the ordinary meaning of tawallud to accidents (aʿrāḍ)?
iqtisad.b: Because accidents have no interior from which another accident can emerge. A movement has no "inside" from which another movement can come forth.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī deny that the movement of a ring literally emerges from the movement of the hand?
iqtisad.b: Since the movement of the hand contains no hidden movement within it, there is nothing from which the ring's movement could literally emerge.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī criticize the claim that the generation of one accident from another is directly observed?
iqtisad.b: He argues that observation only shows that two events occur together or successively. It does not show that one accident literally generates the other.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is actually observed when a hand moves a ring?
iqtisad.b: One only observes that the ring's movement occurs together with or after the hand's movement, not that the hand's movement produces or generates it.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the argument that God could create the hand's movement without the ring's movement if generation were false?
iqtisad.b: He compares it to saying God could create will without knowledge or knowledge without life. Such cases involve necessary conditions, not proof that one thing generates another.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain the relationship between necessary conditions and simultaneous events?
iqtisad.b: He argues that some events necessarily accompany others because they are conditions for them, not because one generates the other.

iqtisad.f: Why must space be vacated before a moving body occupies it according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Because otherwise two bodies would occupy the same place simultaneously, which is impossible. Therefore, vacating the space is a necessary condition for movement.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī deny that one necessary condition generates another event?
iqtisad.b: Because necessary accompaniment due to conditions should not be confused with causal generation. Simultaneous occurrence does not prove one thing creates another.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, into what two categories do alleged cases of generation (tawallud) fall?
iqtisad.b: They are either necessary conditions that cannot be separated, or ordinary concomitants established only by God's customary practice (ʿādah).

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī give of events connected only by God's customary practice (ʿādah)?
iqtisad.b: Cotton burning when near fire and the hand becoming cold when touching ice.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī deny that fire necessarily causes burning?
iqtisad.b: Because burning occurs only through God's customary practice. God could instead create cold in the hand while it touches fire if He willed.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī say God's omnipotence could do contrary to ordinary experience?
iqtisad.b: God could create cold instead of heat during contact with fire, since His power is not inherently limited by ordinary natural sequences.

iqtisad.f: How do proponents of tawallud redefine the doctrine after al-Ghazālī's criticism?
iqtisad.b: They redefine it as the existence of one thing immediately following another, where the first serves as the producer (muwallid) and the second as the generated effect (mutawallad), without implying literal emergence.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the revised definition of tawallud?
iqtisad.b: He argues that it still attributes production to something other than God's power, which contradicts the universal scope of divine omnipotence.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī believe the revised theory of tawallud undermines God's universal power?
iqtisad.b: Because it attributes the occurrence of some events to created things rather than directly to God's power, contradicting the doctrine that every possible event is created by God.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī connect rejection of tawallud with his earlier doctrine of human power?
iqtisad.b: Just as created human power does not independently produce actions, neither do created events independently produce later events; all are directly created by God.

iqtisad.f: What criticism does al-Ghazālī make of the Muʿtazilite theory of tawallud?
iqtisad.b: He says it contains countless inconsistencies, such as claiming that rational reflection generates knowledge while recollection does not.

iqtisad.f: What overall conclusion does al-Ghazālī draw after rejecting tawallud?
iqtisad.b: Every created thing—whether substance or accident, in living beings or inanimate objects—is directly brought into existence by God's power alone.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, do created things produce other created things?
iqtisad.b: No. Created things do not truly produce one another; all creation belongs exclusively to God's power.

iqtisad.f: What is the second divine attribute discussed by al-Ghazālī after power?
iqtisad.b: The second divine attribute is knowledge (al-ʿilm).

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī claim about God's knowledge?
iqtisad.b: God knows all knowable things, including both existent and nonexistent things.

iqtisad.f: Into what two categories does al-Ghazālī divide existing things?
iqtisad.b: Existing things are divided into the eternal (qadīm) and the created (ḥādith).

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say God necessarily knows Himself?
iqtisad.b: Because whoever knows other things must know himself even more perfectly; therefore God certainly knows His own essence and attributes.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī prove that God knows created things?
iqtisad.b: The ordered and perfected creation demonstrates His wisdom and power, just as orderly writing proves the writer possesses knowledge of writing.

iqtisad.f: What analogy does al-Ghazālī use to prove God's knowledge?
iqtisad.b: Just as no rational person doubts that a skilled writer understands writing after seeing well-ordered script, no rational person should doubt God's knowledge after observing the ordered universe.

iqtisad.f: Does al-Ghazālī believe the objects of God's knowledge are finite or infinite?
iqtisad.b: They are infinite because future possibilities are limitless, even if presently existing things are finite.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say God's knowledge extends to infinitely many future possibilities?
iqtisad.b: Because God knows whether every possible future event will occur or not occur, and possible future events have no end.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī illustrate the infinity of God's knowledge using the number two?
iqtisad.b: He notes that the sequence of doubling two (2, 4, 8, 16, 32, etc.) continues without end, and God knows every stage of this infinite progression.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī mention endless numerical doubling?
iqtisad.b: To demonstrate that even one simple mathematical relation contains infinitely many knowable aspects, all of which are known by God.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, is God's knowledge composed of infinitely many separate items?
iqtisad.b: No. Although God's knowledge relates to infinitely many objects, it is itself one single attribute, a point he says will be explained later.

iqtisad.f: What is the third divine attribute discussed by al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: The third divine attribute is life (al-ḥayāh).

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī prove that God is living?
iqtisad.b: He argues that it is self-evident that any being who possesses complete knowledge and power must also be living.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, who denied that God is living?
iqtisad.b: No one who acknowledged that God is knowing and powerful denied that He is living.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī define a living being (ḥayy)?
iqtisad.b: A living being is one that is aware of itself and knows both itself and other things.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī consider the discussion of divine life brief?
iqtisad.b: Because once God's complete knowledge and power are established, His life necessarily follows and requires little further argument.

iqtisad.f: What is the fourth divine attribute discussed by al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: The fourth divine attribute is will (al-irādah).

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī claim regarding God's will?
iqtisad.b: He claims that God wills His actions and that divine will is necessary to specify one possible outcome rather than another.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that God's actions require will?
iqtisad.b: Because God's actions involve choosing one possibility from among equally possible alternatives, and such specification requires a determining factor.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say God's essence alone cannot determine one possibility over another?
iqtisad.b: Because God's essence relates equally to opposite possibilities and therefore cannot by itself explain why one occurs instead of the other.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say divine power alone cannot specify one possibility over another?
iqtisad.b: Because divine power is equally related to all possible alternatives and therefore cannot itself explain why one particular alternative occurs.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the view that God's knowledge alone replaces divine will?
iqtisad.b: Because knowledge merely follows its object as it is and does not produce or determine it. It reflects reality rather than causing it.

iqtisad.f: Which theologian does al-Ghazālī specifically criticize for claiming knowledge replaces will?
iqtisad.b: He criticizes al-Kaʿbī, who held that divine knowledge alone suffices without positing a distinct divine will.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, how does knowledge relate to its object?
iqtisad.b: Knowledge follows and corresponds to its object exactly as it is without altering or determining it.

iqtisad.f: Why can knowledge not determine when the world comes into existence according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Because all possible times for creation are equally possible in themselves, and knowledge merely knows these equal possibilities rather than choosing between them.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what determines the specific time of creation?
iqtisad.b: God's eternal will specifies the particular time, after which divine knowledge knows creation as occurring at that specified time.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī describe the relationship between divine will and divine knowledge?
iqtisad.b: Divine will determines and specifies, while divine knowledge follows what the will has specified and knows it accordingly.

iqtisad.f: Why would denying divine will also undermine divine power according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Because if knowledge alone determined events, power would become unnecessary, just as will would become unnecessary, leading to absurd conclusions.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī argue that denying divine will would also affect human action?
iqtisad.b: If divine knowledge alone determined outcomes, then even human actions would occur without any need for human or divine willing, which is impossible.

iqtisad.f: What objection is raised against al-Ghazālī's doctrine of eternal will?
iqtisad.b: If power requires will to specify one alternative, then eternal will itself seems equally related to opposite alternatives and would require another specifying factor, leading to an infinite regress.

iqtisad.f: Why does the objection claim eternal will cannot determine one alternative by itself?
iqtisad.b: Because eternal will appears equally capable of relating to opposite possibilities, so its specification of one rather than another seems to require an additional cause.

iqtisad.f: What infinite regress does the objection propose against divine will?
iqtisad.b: Every specifying factor would itself require another specifying factor, continuing endlessly without reaching a final explanation.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī characterize this objection?
iqtisad.b: He says it confused many theological schools, but that only Ahl al-Sunnah reached the correct solution.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, into how many major groups did theologians divide concerning the origin of the world?
iqtisad.b: He says they divided into four major groups.

iqtisad.f: What is the first view regarding the world's origin that al-Ghazālī mentions?
iqtisad.b: The philosophers held that the world exists necessarily from God's essence without any additional attribute, making the world eternal like an effect inseparable from its cause.

iqtisad.f: Which examples do the philosophers use to describe the world's relation to God?
iqtisad.b: They compare it to light issuing from the sun or a shadow accompanying a person.

iqtisad.f: Why do philosophers consider the world eternal according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Because they believe it proceeds necessarily from God's eternal essence without any act of choice or will.

iqtisad.f: What is the second theological view described by al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: The Muʿtazilah held that the world was created in time through a created will that itself came into existence without existing in any substrate.

iqtisad.f: How does the Muʿtazilite doctrine explain the world's temporal beginning?
iqtisad.b: It attributes creation to a newly created will that arose and then brought the world into existence at a specific moment.

iqtisad.f: What is the third theological view mentioned by al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Some held that the world was created by a newly occurring will that arose within God's own essence, making God a locus for originated events.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the third view?
iqtisad.b: Because it makes God the subject of newly occurring events, contradicting His eternal and unchanging nature.

iqtisad.f: What is the fourth view, identified by al-Ghazālī as the doctrine of Ahl al-Sunnah?
iqtisad.b: The world came into existence at the exact time eternally specified by God's eternal will, without any newly created will and without any change occurring in God.

iqtisad.f: How does Ahl al-Sunnah explain the temporal creation of the world without change in God?
iqtisad.b: God's eternal will has always specified that the world would exist at a particular time, so creation occurs then without any new attribute or change arising in God.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī believe the Sunni position avoids the difficulties of the other schools?
iqtisad.b: Because it affirms both the eternity of God's attributes and the temporal creation of the world without making God subject to change or denying divine will.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that God's power necessarily extends to every possible thing?
iqtisad.b: Because once it is established that God creates both substances and accidents, it is impossible that He could create them without also being able to create their like. Power over a thing entails power over its equivalent, and since possibilities are unlimited, God's power extends to every possible thing.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say the possible (mumkin) cannot be limited to a finite number?
iqtisad.b: Because there is no limit to possible motions, colors, substances, or future events. There is no possible thing of which it can be said that it lies outside the scope of divine power.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what three branches arise from the doctrine that God's power relates to every possible thing?
iqtisad.b: (1) Whether the opposite of what God knows is within divine power; (2) whether the acts of creatures are also within God's power; and (3) whether generated (mutawallid) effects are produced by creatures or directly by God.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is the dispute over whether the opposite of God's knowledge is "possible" largely verbal?
iqtisad.b: Because it depends on distinguishing what is impossible in itself from what is impossible only because of something external, such as God's eternal knowledge.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain that one thing may be described as necessary, impossible, and possible without contradiction?
iqtisad.b: It is necessary if God's eternal will is assumed to exist, impossible if the divine will for it is assumed absent, and possible when considered solely in itself apart from all external considerations.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, in what sense is the opposite of God's eternal knowledge possible?
iqtisad.b: It is possible in itself, because the thing's essence remains possible, but impossible due to the external consequence of contradicting God's eternal knowledge, not because of its own nature.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī maintain that the opposite of God's eternal knowledge remains an object of divine power?
iqtisad.b: Because divine power relates to the essence of a thing insofar as it is possible in itself. The impossibility arises only from an external factor, namely the impossibility of God's knowledge becoming ignorance.

iqtisad.f: What linguistic argument does al-Ghazālī give for saying that the opposite of God's known decree is still "within God's power"?
iqtisad.b: Ordinary language says a person has power over both motion and rest even though God eternally knows which one will occur. This shows that power is attributed despite only one outcome actually occurring.

iqtisad.f: What two extreme positions regarding human actions does al-Ghazālī reject?
iqtisad.b: He rejects the Jabarites, who deny human power altogether, and the Muʿtazilites, who deny God's power over the voluntary acts of creatures.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the Jabarite denial of human power?
iqtisad.b: Because it contradicts the evident distinction between involuntary movements, such as trembling, and voluntary actions, and it renders religious obligations meaningless.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the Muʿtazilite denial of God's power over human actions?
iqtisad.b: Because it contradicts the doctrine that God alone is the Creator and attributes creation to creatures who themselves do not comprehend the details of what they produce.

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī give to show that animals perform astonishing acts without possessing detailed knowledge?
iqtisad.b: He cites an infant instinctively suckling, a kitten finding its mother's milk, a spider weaving intricate webs, and bees constructing hexagonal honeycombs.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī use the honeycomb example against the Muʿtazilites?
iqtisad.b: The bee constructs geometrically optimal hexagonal cells without understanding geometry, demonstrating that God directs such acts rather than the creature independently creating them through knowledge.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the Sunni position regarding human actions?
iqtisad.b: Human actions are related to two powers: God's power creates both the act and the human's power, while the servant truly possesses power and acquires (kasb) the act.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that one act may legitimately be related to two powers?
iqtisad.b: Because the two powers relate to the act in different ways, so there is no contradiction in both being associated with the same action.

iqtisad.f: What proof does al-Ghazālī offer that both God's power and human power relate to voluntary actions?
iqtisad.b: The obvious distinction between voluntary movement and involuntary trembling proves human power, while the universality of God's power proves that every created event also falls under divine power.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī deny that God's stronger power overrides human power when both relate to one action?
iqtisad.b: Because both powers are considered with respect to the same act of origination, and one relation of origination cannot be stronger than another in that specific respect.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain God's creation of voluntary human actions without denying human power?
iqtisad.b: God creates both the action and the servant's capacity simultaneously. The servant truly possesses power, while God alone originates both the power and the action.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say only God deserves the title "Creator" (Khāliq)?
iqtisad.b: Because God creates both the human power and the action itself, whereas the servant's power does not independently originate the act.

iqtisad.f: What is meant by "kasb" (acquisition) according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Kasb is the special relation between the servant's created power and the action, distinct from true creation, which belongs exclusively to God.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the objection that every power must independently produce its object?
iqtisad.b: He argues that even opponents admit power exists before the act occurs, so power already has a relation to its object before producing it. Therefore, relation does not require independent origination.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject identifying human power that does not independently create with mere impotence?
iqtisad.b: Because the human experiences a real difference between possessing voluntary power and being incapable, even if God's creative power alone originates the act.

iqtisad.f: What question does al-Ghazālī address concerning generated effects (tawallud)?
iqtisad.b: Whether effects such as a ring moving when a hand moves, or water moving when a hand stirs it, are truly generated by created actions or directly created by God.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the Muʿtazilite doctrine of generated effects (tawallud)?
iqtisad.b: Because accidents have no interior from which other accidents could emerge, so saying one accident literally generates another is unintelligible.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain the simultaneous movement of a hand and its ring?
iqtisad.b: Their concurrence is observed, but this does not prove that one movement generates the other. God creates both according to His customary order.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what explains the necessity of certain accompanying events?
iqtisad.b: Some events are genuine conditions, such as vacating a place before another body occupies it, while many other regular successions are simply God's established habit (ʿādah).

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī use to illustrate God's customary order rather than intrinsic causation?
iqtisad.b: Cotton burning near fire and a hand becoming cold when touching ice occur by God's customary practice, not because created things possess independent causal power.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the refined Muʿtazilite definition of generated effects?
iqtisad.b: Even if generation merely means that one event follows another through it, this still removes those effects from God's universal power and therefore remains unacceptable.

iqtisad.f: What conclusion does al-Ghazālī reach about all created substances and accidents?
iqtisad.b: Every substance and accident, whether occurring in living beings or inanimate objects, is directly brought into existence by God's power alone.

iqtisad.f: What is al-Ghazālī's main proof that God possesses knowledge?
iqtisad.b: The ordered and perfected creation proves its Maker possesses knowledge, just as orderly writing proves the writer knows the art of writing.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say God necessarily knows Himself?
iqtisad.b: Whoever knows others necessarily knows himself even more perfectly, so God's knowledge of creation implies perfect knowledge of His own essence and attributes.

iqtisad.f: Does al-Ghazālī believe God's knowledge has a finite number of objects?
iqtisad.b: No. God's knowledge encompasses infinitely many possible future events, relations, and numerical possibilities without limit.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī illustrate the infinity of God's knowledge using mathematics?
iqtisad.b: He points to the endless doubling of numbers, showing that even the successive doubles of two continue without end and all are known by God.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī regard God's life (ḥayāh) as self-evident?
iqtisad.b: Because everyone who admits God is knowing and powerful necessarily admits He is living, since life is that by which one is aware and knows.

iqtisad.f: What definition of "living" (ḥayy) does al-Ghazālī employ?
iqtisad.b: A living being is one who is aware of himself and knows both himself and others.

iqtisad.f: What is al-Ghazālī's principal proof that God possesses will (irādah)?
iqtisad.b: Every created thing is specified in one way rather than another among equally possible alternatives, and this specification requires a determining attribute distinct from power and knowledge.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī deny that divine knowledge alone can determine one possibility over another?
iqtisad.b: Because knowledge merely corresponds to what exists as it is; it follows the object rather than causing or specifying it.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why can neither God's essence nor His power alone explain specification?
iqtisad.b: Because both stand in equal relation to opposite possibilities and therefore cannot by themselves explain why one alternative rather than another occurs.

iqtisad.f: What major objection against divine will does al-Ghazālī discuss?
iqtisad.b: If will determines one alternative over another, what determines the will itself, leading seemingly to an infinite regress.

iqtisad.f: What four schools does al-Ghazālī distinguish regarding the origin of the world?
iqtisad.b: The philosophers (eternal world), the Muʿtazilites (created by a newly originated will outside God), those who say a new will arises within God, and the Sunnis (created through God's eternal will).

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the philosophers' doctrine of an eternal world?
iqtisad.b: Because an act is, by definition, something that comes into existence after not existing, and an eternal act is therefore contradictory.

iqtisad.f: What additional philosophical difficulties does al-Ghazālī raise against the philosophers?
iqtisad.b: They cannot explain why the heavenly spheres move in one direction rather than the opposite, nor why particular points of the outer sphere became its poles rather than any other points.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the Muʿtazilite doctrine of a newly created will outside God?
iqtisad.b: Because a will not existing in God cannot make Him willing, and the creation of that will itself requires another determining will, producing infinite regress.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the view that new acts of will arise within God?
iqtisad.b: Because it makes God the subject of originated events, implying that He Himself would be originated.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the question, "Why did God's eternal will specify this possibility rather than its equal opposite?"
iqtisad.b: Will is, by definition, the attribute whose very function is to specify one of two equal possibilities. Asking why it specifies is like asking why knowledge knows or why possibility is possible.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is the Sunni doctrine of eternal will superior to the other views?
iqtisad.b: Because it avoids eternal creation, avoids originated attributes in or outside God, and terminates the infinite regress by affirming an eternal will that specifies events.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, to what does God's will relate?
iqtisad.b: God's eternal will relates to every created event, because every created thing brought into existence by divine power also requires divine will to specify it.

iqtisad.f: What conclusion does al-Ghazālī draw regarding sins, disbelief, and evil?
iqtisad.b: Since they are created events, they necessarily occur by God's eternal will, though this does not mean He commands or approves of them.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī criticize the Muʿtazilite claim that God does not will sins?
iqtisad.b: He argues that if most events in the world occur contrary to God's will, this falsely portrays God as weak and unable to accomplish what He wills.

iqtisad.f: What objections does al-Ghazālī postpone answering regarding God's willing of sins?
iqtisad.b: He postpones explaining how God may will what He forbids, command what He does not will, and why willing evil does not imply foolishness, promising to resolve these under the discussion of good and evil.

iqtisad.f: Which two divine attributes does al-Ghazālī discuss in this section?
iqtisad.b: He discusses the divine attributes of hearing (samʿ) and sight (baṣar), affirming that God is All-Hearing and All-Seeing.

iqtisad.f: What is al-Ghazālī's overall claim regarding God's hearing and sight?
iqtisad.b: He claims that the Creator is truly Hearing and Seeing, and that both revelation and reason establish these attributes.

iqtisad.f: What scriptural evidence does al-Ghazālī cite for God's hearing and sight?
iqtisad.b: He cites verses such as "He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing" and Abraham's عليه السلام statement, "Why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees nor benefits you in the least?"

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī use Abraham's عليه السلام argument against idol worship to prove God's hearing and sight?
iqtisad.b: Abraham's عليه السلام argument would only be valid if the true God actually possesses hearing and sight, making these genuine divine attributes absent from idols.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the claim that "hearing" and "seeing" merely mean "knowledge"?
iqtisad.b: He argues that scriptural words should retain their apparent meanings unless those meanings are impossible, and since hearing and sight are not impossible for God, there is no justification for reinterpreting them as mere knowledge.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject interpreting God's hearing and sight as simply His knowledge?
iqtisad.b: Because no rational impossibility requires abandoning the literal meanings, and the consensus of Muslims understood these attributes as real, distinct attributes.

iqtisad.f: What objection is raised against affirming eternal hearing and sight?
iqtisad.b: If they are originated, God would become the locus of originated attributes; if eternal, how can God hear sounds or see things before they exist?

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the Muʿtazilite objection that eternal hearing and sight cannot relate to future events?
iqtisad.b: He argues that since the Muʿtazilah already affirm God's eternal knowledge of future events without change, the same reasoning equally applies to hearing and sight.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the philosopher who denies God's knowledge of particular temporal events?
iqtisad.b: He first establishes that God's eternal knowledge encompasses temporal particulars, and then extends the same argument by analogy to hearing and sight.

iqtisad.f: What rational argument does al-Ghazālī use to prove that God must possess hearing and sight?
iqtisad.b: The Creator must be more perfect than His creation, and hearing and sight are perfections; therefore God must possess them.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that the Creator must be more perfect than creatures?
iqtisad.b: Because reason and revelation unanimously affirm that it is impossible for creatures to possess a perfection absent from their Creator.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī regard hearing and sight as genuine perfections?
iqtisad.b: Because they provide a greater degree of perception than knowledge alone, increasing clarity and disclosure.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain that sight is a perfection beyond knowledge?
iqtisad.b: A person who first knows something and later sees it gains an additional degree of certainty and clarity, showing that sight perfects knowledge.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why would denying hearing and sight to God imply imperfection?
iqtisad.b: Because hearing and sight are genuine perfections; denying them would either make them imperfections or neither perfection nor imperfection, both of which are absurd.

iqtisad.f: What objection is raised from the senses of smell, taste, and touch?
iqtisad.b: If hearing and sight are perfections because they increase perception, then smell, taste, and touch should also be affirmed as divine attributes.

iqtisad.f: How do many Sunni theologians answer the objection concerning smell, taste, and touch?
iqtisad.b: They affirm that God possesses additional modes of perfect perception beyond hearing, sight, and knowledge, while denying the bodily mechanisms normally associated with those senses.

iqtisad.f: Why do Sunni theologians refuse to name additional divine perceptive attributes such as smell or taste?
iqtisad.b: Because revelation explicitly names only knowledge, hearing, and sight, so they do not introduce additional divine names without scriptural evidence.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, are bodily mechanisms such as physical contact required for God's perception?
iqtisad.b: No. God perceives without bodily contact, physical organs, or ordinary sensory conditions.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī compare God's sight to created sight regarding physical direction?
iqtisad.b: Just as God may see without physical confrontation or direction, He may possess perfect perception without the bodily conditions required by creatures.

iqtisad.f: What principle governs which forms of perception may be affirmed for God?
iqtisad.b: Every form of perception that is pure perfection may be affirmed, while every form that entails deficiency or originated bodily conditions must be denied.

iqtisad.f: What further objection is raised concerning pleasure and pain?
iqtisad.b: If lacking sensory perception is an imperfection, then should God also possess pleasure, pain, desire, and appetite, since lacking them is a deficiency in creatures?

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī deny pain, pleasure, and appetite of the created kind to God?
iqtisad.b: Because they imply origination, need, dependence, and bodily conditions, all of which are impossible for God.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī regard pain as an imperfection rather than a perfection?
iqtisad.b: Pain depends on bodily injury and contact, both of which are defects and signs of createdness.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain pleasure in created beings?
iqtisad.b: Pleasure ultimately results either from the removal of pain or from attaining something one previously lacked and desired.

iqtisad.f: Why is desire (shahwah) impossible for God according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Because desire means seeking something absent, while nothing can be absent from God's possession or power.

iqtisad.f: Why can God never experience pleasure through acquiring something?
iqtisad.b: Because pleasure based on acquisition presupposes previous lack or need, whereas God lacks nothing whatsoever.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is appetite impossible for God?
iqtisad.b: Appetite presupposes deficiency, need, and the pursuit of what is missing, all of which contradict God's absolute perfection.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain statements that lacking pain or appetite is a defect in creatures?
iqtisad.b: Such things are only considered perfections relative to avoiding greater harms in created beings; they are not intrinsic perfections applicable to God.

iqtisad.f: Why are knowledge, hearing, and sight unlike appetite or pain in al-Ghazālī's theology?
iqtisad.b: Knowledge, hearing, and sight are intrinsic perfections in themselves, whereas appetite, pleasure, and pain depend upon prior deficiency or bodily need.

iqtisad.f: What overall principle does al-Ghazālī establish regarding divine attributes of perception?
iqtisad.b: Every attribute that constitutes pure perfection without implying createdness belongs to God, while every attribute dependent upon need, deficiency, or bodily conditions must be denied.

iqtisad.f: What is the main rational argument for affirming that Allah is described with speech (kalām)?
iqtisad.b: Speech is a perfection. It is impossible for a perfection to belong to the creature while being denied of the Creator. Therefore, Allah must be described with speech.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject proving Allah's speech merely by saying that people are commanded and prohibited?
iqtisad.b: Because that argument assumes from the outset that Allah can issue commands and prohibitions, which is precisely the point under dispute. It therefore begs the question.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject proving Allah's speech solely through consensus (ijmāʿ) or the Prophet's ﷺ testimony?
iqtisad.b: Because consensus depends upon the Prophet ﷺ, and prophethood itself presupposes that Allah can speak. Someone who denies Allah's speech will also deny the possibility of divine revelation, making such an argument circular.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what are the three possibilities regarding speech, and which does he affirm for Allah?
iqtisad.b: Speech is either (1) sounds and letters, (2) the power to produce sounds and letters, or (3) an eternal inner speech (kalām al-nafs). Al-Ghazālī affirms only the third for Allah.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī deny that Allah's speech consists of sounds and letters?
iqtisad.b: Because sounds and letters are originated events (ḥawādith). If they existed in Allah's essence, He would become a locus of originated events, which is impossible.

iqtisad.f: Why is Allah's mere ability to create sounds not sufficient to make Him "speaking" (mutakallim)?
iqtisad.b: Because being able to create speech is different from possessing the attribute of speech itself. Otherwise, Allah would only be called speaking by producing created sounds, not by possessing eternal speech.

iqtisad.f: What is meant by kalām al-nafs (inner speech) according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: It is an internal meaning existing within the speaker that is distinct from spoken sounds and letters. Spoken words merely indicate this inner speech.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī argue that inner speech exists in human beings?
iqtisad.b: People naturally say, "I composed words within myself," or "He has something in his mind that he intends to say." This common usage shows that inner speech is distinct from outward speech.

iqtisad.f: What poetic evidence does al-Ghazālī cite to support the existence of inner speech?
iqtisad.b: He cites the verse: "Speech is in the heart, and the tongue was only made as its guide," showing that speech exists internally before verbal expression.

iqtisad.f: What objection does al-Ghazālī answer regarding inner speech?
iqtisad.b: His opponents argue that what people call inner speech is nothing more than knowledge, memory of words, and mental arrangement of meanings, rather than a distinct attribute.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī's opponents, what constitutes inner speech?
iqtisad.b: They claim it consists only of knowledge of meanings, knowledge of words, and the mental arrangement of these meanings and words by thought, with no additional reality beyond these.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī distinguish inner speech from the intention to communicate?
iqtisad.b: The intention to communicate is merely the will to indicate a meaning, whereas every indication requires something already existing to be indicated. That indicated reality is the inner speech itself.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say inner speech cannot simply be the intention that someone obey a command?
iqtisad.b: Because a person may issue a command while not wanting it to be obeyed, showing that command and will are distinct.

iqtisad.f: What example does al-Ghazālī use to show that command and will are not identical?
iqtisad.b: A man who wants to prove his servant's disobedience before a ruler commands the servant to stand while actually hoping he will refuse. He truly commands, yet does not will compliance.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what does the command "Stand!" signify besides the intention to communicate?
iqtisad.b: It signifies an internal demand or command existing within the speaker, which is the true speech (kalām), distinct from merely wishing to communicate or desiring obedience.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī conclude that Allah's speech is neither sounds nor mere will?
iqtisad.b: Because sounds imply origination, while will is distinct from command. Therefore, Allah's speech is an eternal internal speech that is neither created sounds nor identical with His will.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī distinguish Allah's speech from created spoken language?
iqtisad.b: Created language consists of sounds and letters that point to meanings, whereas Allah's eternal speech is the underlying meaning itself, not the created verbal expression.

iqtisad.f: What is the overall Sunni doctrine of Allah's speech that al-Ghazālī defends?
iqtisad.b: Allah is eternally described with speech (kalām nafsī), which is neither sounds nor letters, is distinct from knowledge and will, and is indicated by created expressions and revelation without itself being created.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī refute the claim that a person who commands while not wanting obedience is not truly issuing a command?
iqtisad.b: He argues that such a person is genuinely issuing a command. If he were not, his command could not serve as evidence or excuse in the situation he intends.

iqtisad.f: What example does al-Ghazālī use to prove that command (amr) is distinct from the will for obedience?
iqtisad.b: He describes a master who commands his servant to stand before the king while secretly hoping the servant disobeys so that he can demonstrate the servant's disobedience to the king.

iqtisad.f: Why does the master's argument before the king prove that command is different from the will for obedience?
iqtisad.b: Because the master's excuse depends on the fact that he truly commanded the servant, even though he did not desire the servant to obey. If command required willing obedience, his excuse would fail.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī use a legal (fiqh) example to distinguish command from will?
iqtisad.b: He says that if such a master swore by triple divorce that he had commanded the servant, every Muslim jurist would affirm that he truly issued a command. They would not deny it merely because he did not want obedience.

iqtisad.f: What conclusion does al-Ghazālī draw from the king and legal examples regarding command?
iqtisad.b: They demonstrate that the meaning signified by a command exists independently of the will for obedience, proving that command is a distinct reality.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the relationship between speech (kalām), knowledge, and will?
iqtisad.b: Speech is a distinct attribute, different from knowledge, will, and belief. It cannot be reduced to any of them.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī affirm an eternal divine speech?
iqtisad.b: Since speech is a distinct perfection that does not consist of sounds or letters, it can exist eternally as one of Allah's attributes without implying origination.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what are spoken letters and sounds in relation to Allah's eternal speech?
