iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does he reject the claim that human beings truly deserve reward through their own obedience?
iqtisad.b: Because every act of obedience depends entirely upon Allah's gifts—including existence, ability, will, sound limbs, and all enabling causes. Since these are all from Allah, independent merit cannot be claimed.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what ultimately enables every act of obedience performed by a servant?
iqtisad.b: Every act of obedience depends upon Allah's prior gifts: creating the servant, granting ability, will, physical health, and all the conditions necessary for performing the act.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī in al-Iqtiṣād fī al-Iʿtiqād, what is meant by ḥasan (good) in its most general sense?
iqtisad.b: A good (ḥasan) action is one that accords with or fulfills the purpose, interest, or objective (gharad) of the one to whom it is related. It has no meaning beyond its agreement with that purpose.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is meant by qabīḥ (bad/ugly) in its most general sense?
iqtisad.b: A bad (qabīḥ) action is one that opposes or frustrates the purpose or objective (gharad) of the one to whom it is related. It has no meaning beyond its opposition to that purpose.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is meant by ʿabath (futility)?
iqtisad.b: Futility (ʿabath) is an action that serves no purpose whatsoever for the agent—it neither benefits nor harms him.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, who is called ʿābith (one who acts futilely) and who is called safīh (foolish)?
iqtisad.b: One who performs a purposeless act is called a ʿābith (one who acts futilely). One who performs a harmful or bad act is called safīh (foolish), and this designation is even more appropriate than calling him a mere ʿābith.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that good and bad are relative rather than intrinsic qualities?
iqtisad.b: Because whether an action is called good or bad depends on whose interests it serves or harms. The same action may be good for one person and bad for another, showing that goodness and badness are relational rather than essential properties.

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī give to demonstrate that goodness and badness are relative?
iqtisad.b: He gives several examples: (1) An adulterer sees adultery as desirable, while a religious person condemns it. (2) The enemies of a king praise his assassin, whereas his supporters condemn him. (3) Some people naturally prefer dark complexions while others prefer fair ones.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say that colours differ from goodness and badness?
iqtisad.b: Colours are intrinsic qualities that do not change according to different observers. A thing cannot be black for one person and white for another, whereas an action can be good for one person and bad for another because goodness and badness are relational.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what are the three usages of the term ḥasan (good)?
iqtisad.b: (1) Everything that fulfills any purpose, whether worldly or otherworldly. (2) Specifically, what fulfills one's purpose in the Hereafter—that is, what the Sharīʿah praises and promises reward for (the Ashʿarī usage). (3) Whatever God does, since His acts are beyond blame or liability, even though He has no personal purpose to fulfill.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what are the two meanings of ḥikmah (wisdom)?
iqtisad.b: (1) Complete knowledge of the proper order and reality of things. (2) The ability to produce, arrange, perfect, and establish that proper order in action.

iqtisad.f: What is the first illusion (ghalaṭ) that leads people to misunderstand goodness and badness, according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: People judge an action to be absolutely bad merely because it conflicts with their own interests, forgetting that it may serve the interests of others or even their own interests under different circumstances.

iqtisad.f: What is the second illusion identified by al-Ghazālī regarding moral judgment?
iqtisad.b: Because something is harmful in almost every circumstance, people mistakenly conclude that it is intrinsically and universally bad, overlooking the rare cases in which it serves a beneficial purpose.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī use lying to illustrate the second illusion?
iqtisad.b: People often say lying is intrinsically evil because they have been trained from childhood to reject it absolutely. In reality, lying is only generally harmful, while in rare situations it may serve an important benefit.

iqtisad.f: What is the third illusion that distorts human judgment according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: People mistakenly reverse a constant association. Because a particular thing is frequently accompanied by another, they assume the reverse association always holds as well.

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī give for the third illusion of mistaken association?
iqtisad.b: A person bitten by a snake fears any striped rope; someone is disgusted by yellow pudding because it resembles filth; people dislike names associated with unattractive groups even when applied to attractive individuals.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why do many theological disputes persist despite clear rational proofs?
iqtisad.b: Because people become emotionally attached to inherited opinions. They judge ideas by the schools associated with them rather than by the evidence itself, calling supporting arguments "proofs" and opposing arguments "doubts."

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the proper method for seeking theological truth?
iqtisad.b: One should suspend prior commitment, examine the evidence itself, accept what the evidence establishes as true, and reject its opposite, rather than beginning with inherited doctrines.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain why a person may admire rescuing a stranger even without expecting any worldly or religious benefit?
iqtisad.b: Human beings naturally possess sympathy and imagine themselves in the victim's place. This emotional disposition makes rescue agreeable even without conscious expectation of reward.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what additional factors may incline someone to perform apparently altruistic actions?
iqtisad.b: Habitual desire for praise, deeply rooted psychological associations, imagination, emotional conditioning, and natural human sympathy all influence such actions, even when no immediate benefit is consciously expected.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain psychological conditioning using poetry about beloved places?
iqtisad.b: People love places because they associate them with pleasant memories, beloved persons, and youthful experiences. The affection is transferred from the associated experiences to the places themselves.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why do imagination and habit often overpower rational judgment?
iqtisad.b: God created many human faculties to respond automatically to imagination and habitual associations. Thus bodily and emotional reactions frequently follow imagined associations even when reason knows them to be false.

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī give to show that bodily faculties obey imagination rather than reason?
iqtisad.b: Salivation when imagining delicious food, sexual arousal when imagining a beautiful person despite intending abstinence, fear of harmless objects resembling dangerous ones, and emotional attachment to familiar places.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why might someone admire martyrdom or steadfastness under torture?
iqtisad.b: Because he expects either divine reward or lasting honour and praise among people, both of which serve perceived purposes and therefore explain the preference without appealing to intrinsic moral qualities.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why might someone refuse to break a covenant even when doing so would save his life?
iqtisad.b: Because of the expectation of praise, honour, or psychological attachment to faithfulness that has become deeply ingrained through repeated association.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what conclusion does he draw from his analysis of human psychology?
iqtisad.b: Human preferences ultimately trace back to purposes, interests, imagination, habit, and psychological conditioning. They do not establish that goodness and badness are objective qualities existing independently in actions themselves.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the first theological claim regarding God's actions after discussing the meanings of obligation, goodness, and badness?
iqtisad.b: God is not obligated to create creation, nor to impose legal obligations (taklīf) upon them. Both creation and legislation are entirely permissible acts, not duties imposed upon Him.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī define wājib (obligatory) when refuting the Muʿtazilah's claim that God must create and legislate?
iqtisad.b: A duty is either (1) something whose omission brings harm, or (2) something whose opposite is impossible. Since neither applies to God regarding creation and legislation, they cannot be obligatory upon Him.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the claim that God must create because creation benefits creatures?
iqtisad.b: Benefit to creatures does not impose obligation upon God. Even if creation benefits them, this alone cannot make it obligatory unless "obligation" is redefined with a new meaning, which must first be explained.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does he reject the claim that creating and testing creatures is necessary for their ultimate benefit?
iqtisad.b: If God wished to bestow bliss, He could have created them directly in Paradise without hardship or obligation. Therefore, testing is not necessary to confer benefit.

iqtisad.f: What argument does al-Ghazālī use against the claim that reward after earned obedience is better than reward granted freely?
iqtisad.b: He argues that considering freely bestowed divine favour inferior reflects arrogance toward God. Furthermore, every act of obedience itself depends entirely on God's grace, so even earned reward ultimately rests upon His favour.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is his second theological claim regarding taklīf (legal obligation)?
iqtisad.b: God may obligate His servants with duties that they are able to perform and also with duties that they are unable to perform.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī define taklīf?
iqtisad.b: Taklīf is a form of divine address (khiṭāb): it consists of speech from one who commands to one who understands, concerning something intelligible. The commanded act need not be possible for the speech itself to qualify as taklīf.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that commanding the impossible is conceptually possible?
iqtisad.b: Because the essence of a command is merely speech or an internal command directed to someone capable of understanding it. Impossibility of fulfillment does not make the command itself inconceivable.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the objection that commanding the impossible is futile (ʿabath)?
iqtisad.b: He argues that it may serve purposes unknown to us, such as testing, manifesting obedience, or other divine wisdom. Therefore, one cannot claim with certainty that it is purposeless.

iqtisad.f: What two scriptural examples does al-Ghazālī cite to support the possibility of commanding what will not occur?
iqtisad.b: Abraham عليه السلام was commanded to sacrifice his son before the command was withdrawn, and Abū Jahl was commanded to believe even though God had already informed that he would never believe.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is his third theological claim regarding innocent creatures?
iqtisad.b: God has the power to inflict pain upon innocent animals, children, or those free from sin without becoming obligated to compensate or reward them afterward.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the Muʿtazilī claim that God must reward every innocent creature for its suffering?
iqtisad.b: He argues that this rests on an incorrect concept of obligation. Since no obligation can be imposed upon God merely because creatures suffer, no such reward is necessary by reason alone.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is God never described as unjust (ẓālim)?
iqtisad.b: Injustice (ẓulm) is impossible for God because it can only occur when someone wrongfully disposes of another's property or disobeys someone whose command is binding upon him. Since everything belongs to God and no one has authority over Him, the conditions necessary for injustice can never exist in His case.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī compare the denial of injustice from God to other forms of negation?
iqtisad.b: He compares it to denying heedlessness (ghaflah) of a wall or purposelessness (ʿabath) of the wind. Such descriptions are denied because the subject does not possess the conditions that make those qualities applicable in the first place.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, when can a human being properly be described as unjust (ẓālim)?
iqtisad.b: A human is unjust either by violating another person's rights or property or by violating God's command. Since humans can possess both of these conditions, injustice applies to them, unlike God.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what should be concluded if someone defines ẓulm (injustice) differently from its accepted meaning?
iqtisad.b: If injustice is given another meaning, then that meaning must first be explained. Otherwise, it is unintelligible and cannot meaningfully be affirmed or denied of God.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the fourth theological claim concerning God's actions?
iqtisad.b: God is not obligated to do what is most beneficial (al-aṣlaḥ) for His servants. He may do whatever He wills and judge however He pleases.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the Muʿtazilite doctrine that God must always do what is most beneficial (al-aṣlaḥ) for His servants?
iqtisad.b: Because no obligation can be imposed upon God. The same arguments proving that nothing is obligatory upon God also refute the claim that He must always choose what is most beneficial for His creatures.

iqtisad.f: What example does al-Ghazālī use to argue against the Muʿtazilite doctrine of al-aṣlaḥ (doing what is most beneficial)?
iqtisad.b: He imagines three children: one dies as a Muslim before puberty, one reaches adulthood as a believing Muslim, and one reaches adulthood as an unbeliever. Their different eternal outcomes create difficulties for the claim that God always does what is most beneficial for every individual.

iqtisad.f: How does the Muslim child who died before puberty challenge the Muʿtazilite doctrine of al-aṣlaḥ in al-Ghazālī's argument?
iqtisad.b: The child asks why he was denied the higher rank earned by the adult believer. If God replies that extending his life would have led him to disbelief, this explanation creates a greater difficulty when considering the unbeliever.

iqtisad.f: How does the unbelieving adult challenge the Muʿtazilite doctrine of al-aṣlaḥ in al-Ghazālī's argument?
iqtisad.b: The unbeliever asks why God did not allow him to die before puberty, since God supposedly knew he would disbelieve and be eternally punished. Dying young would have been more beneficial for him than eternal punishment.

iqtisad.f: What conclusion does al-Ghazālī draw from the example of the three children regarding al-aṣlaḥ?
iqtisad.b: The example shows that it is impossible to maintain consistently that God is obligated to choose what is absolutely most beneficial for every individual servant.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the fifth theological claim concerning reward and punishment?
iqtisad.b: God is not obligated to reward the obedient. If He wills, He may reward them, punish them, forgive the unbelievers, punish the believers, or even refrain from resurrecting them, provided He does not contradict His own promise.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the only sense in which reward becomes obligatory upon God?
iqtisad.b: Reward becomes obligatory only because God has promised it. Breaking His promise would amount to falsehood, which is impossible for Him.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the claim that imposing obligations without granting reward is morally wrong?
iqtisad.b: He argues that if "wrong" means contrary to God's interests, God has no interests. If it means contrary to human interests, that standard cannot be imposed upon God, since human notions of good and bad do not bind Him.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī use the master-servant relationship to argue that reward is not owed for obedience?
iqtisad.b: A servant serves his master because he is a servant, not because he deserves payment. If every service required compensation, the very concept of servitude would disappear.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī argue against the Muʿtazilite claim that God must reward people for thanking Him?
iqtisad.b: If thanking God deserves reward, then that reward itself would require further gratitude, which would require another reward, leading to an infinite regress of obligations and rewards.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does he criticize the Muʿtazilite doctrine that unbelievers and major sinners must be punished eternally?
iqtisad.b: He argues that it contradicts generosity, mercy, common reason, ordinary human practice, and the preference people naturally have for forgiveness over endless vengeance.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī argue from ordinary human judgment that forgiveness is preferable to punishment?
iqtisad.b: Human beings generally praise those who forgive more than those who take revenge. Mercy and pardon are admired, whereas prolonged vengeance is not regarded as the noblest course.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is the analogy between human justice and divine punishment fundamentally flawed?
iqtisad.b: Human beings may seek revenge because wrongdoing harms or diminishes them, whereas neither disbelief nor obedience affects God's majesty or perfection in any way.

iqtisad.f: What criticism does al-Ghazālī make of eternal punishment for a single act of disbelief or sin?
iqtisad.b: He argues that regarding endless punishment for a single finite act as intrinsically appropriate reflects a profoundly defective moral intuition rather than sound reason.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, under what circumstance can punishment be considered reasonable from the standpoint of human purposes?
iqtisad.b: Punishment is reasonable when it prevents future harm or deters future wrongdoing. If it serves no future benefit and merely inflicts suffering for past actions, it has no rational purpose from the human perspective.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why would punishment solely for past wrongdoing be considered purposeless from the human point of view?
iqtisad.b: Because past actions cannot be undone, and if punishment produces no future benefit for anyone, it merely causes additional suffering without achieving any useful purpose.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what second argument could be given for why human beings sometimes regard punishment as appropriate?
iqtisad.b: If the victim has been harmed, his anger is itself painful, and punishing the offender relieves that pain. Since it is more fitting for the offender to suffer than the victim, punishment may seem preferable, although this reflects weakness of reason and domination by anger.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does he reject making punishment obligatory merely for past wrongdoing?
iqtisad.b: Because punishment that serves no future benefit, prevents no future harm, and relieves no injury is extremely ugly (qabīḥ). Both making punishment obligatory and making its omission obligatory are based on imagined human purposes, whereas God is transcendent above such purposes.

iqtisad.f: What is al-Ghazālī's sixth claim concerning human obligations before revelation?
iqtisad.b: If revelation had not come, human beings would not have been obligated to know God or thank Him merely by reason alone.

iqtisad.f: Which theological school does al-Ghazālī oppose in his sixth claim about rational obligation?
iqtisad.b: He opposes the Muʿtazilah, who held that reason by itself imposes obligations such as knowing God and thanking Him.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why must reason only obligate actions that have some benefit?
iqtisad.b: Because reason does not command pointless acts (ʿabath). An action entirely devoid of benefit would be vain, and reason does not require vain acts.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why can no benefit of knowing or thanking God return to God Himself?
iqtisad.b: Because God is exalted above receiving benefits or advantages from the actions of His creatures.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does present-life benefit not justify rational obligation to know or thank God?
iqtisad.b: Because seeking such knowledge involves effort and hardship without any immediate worldly benefit.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does expected reward in the Hereafter not establish a rational obligation to know or thank God?
iqtisad.b: Because reason alone cannot know that God will reward such actions; it is equally conceivable, apart from revelation, that He might punish them instead.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the argument that reason naturally fears punishment for failing to thank God?
iqtisad.b: He accepts that human nature avoids even possible harm, but this psychological inclination does not prove that reason itself imposes an objective obligation.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does al-Ghazālī say God's relation to gratitude and ingratitude differs from that of human beings?
iqtisad.b: Unlike human beings, who delight in gratitude and are hurt by ingratitude, God is unaffected by both gratitude and ingratitude, so reason cannot prefer one over the other on God's behalf.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what first counter-possibility does he raise against rationally obligating gratitude toward God?
iqtisad.b: A person might think that God intended him to enjoy His blessings rather than burden himself with speculative inquiry and acts that bring God no benefit.

iqtisad.f: What analogy does al-Ghazālī use to criticize unaided rational inquiry into God's attributes?
iqtisad.b: He compares it to someone who repays a king's favor by prying into the king's private life, secrets, habits, and household, an intrusion deserving punishment rather than praise.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why does he say that investigating God's deepest attributes cannot be assumed rationally obligatory?
iqtisad.b: Because such knowledge resembles access to royal secrets and requires a special rank; reason alone cannot establish that every servant deserves such a station.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what does he conclude about the Muʿtazilite belief in rational obligation after presenting these counterexamples?
iqtisad.b: He concludes that their position rests on ingrained habits and assumptions that can be opposed by equally plausible counter-assumptions.

iqtisad.f: What objection does al-Ghazālī address concerning proving prophethood if reason imposes no obligation to investigate miracles?
iqtisad.b: The objection claims that if examining miracles is not rationally obligatory before revelation, a prophet could never establish his prophethood because people could refuse to investigate his miracle.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, how does he answer the objection that denying rational obligation undermines prophethood?
iqtisad.b: He says the objection misunderstands obligation: obligation is the preference for an action because of attached reward or punishment, and only God creates that preference by attaching consequences.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, who is the true source of obligation (ījāb)?
iqtisad.b: God alone, because He makes an action preferable by attaching reward or punishment to it.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the difference between the source of obligation and the means of knowing it?
iqtisad.b: The source of obligation is God, who establishes reward and punishment, whereas the means of knowing the obligation is the evidence that informs people of God's ruling.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, must a person already know that an obligation exists before it truly exists?
iqtisad.b: No. An obligation may exist before someone knows it, provided the means of discovering it are available.

iqtisad.f: What analogy does al-Ghazālī use to explain the Prophet's ﷺ role in guiding people to faith?
iqtisad.b: He compares the Prophet ﷺ to a physician who warns a patient not to drink a certain medicine because it is deadly and shows him how to verify the warning through a test. The physician informs and guides but does not himself create the danger or the obligation to avoid it.

iqtisad.f: What analogy does al-Ghazālī use to explain the Prophet's ﷺ role in calling people to faith?
iqtisad.b: He compares the Prophet ﷺ to a physician who tells a patient that one medicine is deadly and another is healing, while showing him how he can verify the claim through experience.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī's analogy, what attitude does the physician have toward the patient's survival?
iqtisad.b: The physician says that neither he nor his master gains or loses anything whether the patient lives or dies, because they are independent of him. Likewise, God has no need of His creatures.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what would happen if the patient refused to test the physician's claim until he first proved that reason obligated him to do so?
iqtisad.b: He would destroy himself through his own refusal, while causing no harm to the physician.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the Prophet's ﷺ role regarding faith and obedience?
iqtisad.b: The Prophet ﷺ informs people that faith and obedience lead to salvation, disbelief and disobedience lead to destruction, and directs them to the means of verifying his truthfulness.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, who benefits or suffers from accepting or rejecting the Prophet's ﷺ guidance?
iqtisad.b: The benefit or harm returns entirely to the individual; God is completely independent of whether people are saved or destroyed.

iqtisad.f: What objection does al-Ghazālī answer regarding the role of reason in obligation?
iqtisad.b: The objection claims that reason itself becomes the obligating force because hearing the Prophet's ﷺ warning makes a person fear punishment and therefore compels him to investigate.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the true meaning of obligation (wujūb)?
iqtisad.b: Obligation is the predominance or preference of performing an action over leaving it.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, who is the true obligating agent (al-mūjib)?
iqtisad.b: God alone is the obligating agent because He is the One who establishes the preference by attaching reward and punishment to actions.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the Prophet's ﷺ function in relation to obligation?
iqtisad.b: The Prophet ﷺ does not create obligation but merely reports God's ruling and warns people of its consequences.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what function does the miracle (muʿjizah) serve?
iqtisad.b: The miracle serves as evidence proving the truthfulness of the Prophet's ﷺ claim.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what role does rational inquiry (naẓar) play in faith?
iqtisad.b: Rational inquiry is the means by which a person recognizes the miracle and thereby knows that the Prophet ﷺ is truthful.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what role does the intellect (ʿaql) play in accepting revelation?
iqtisad.b: The intellect is the instrument used for reasoning, understanding the Prophet's ﷺ message, and recognizing the danger being warned against.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what role does human nature (ṭabʿ) play after understanding the Prophet's ﷺ warning?
iqtisad.b: Human nature motivates a person to avoid danger and seek salvation once the danger has been understood through reason.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is reason alone insufficient to establish obligation?
iqtisad.b: Because reason can understand the Prophet's ﷺ message, but it cannot by itself establish the preference of one course of action over another without God's declaration.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the proper distribution of roles in establishing religious obligation?
iqtisad.b: God establishes obligation; the Prophet ﷺ reports it; the miracle verifies the Prophet ﷺ; reason understands the verification; and human nature motivates a person to pursue salvation.

iqtisad.f: What is al-Ghazālī's seventh theological claim concerning prophethood?
iqtisad.b: The sending of prophets is possible, neither impossible nor obligatory upon God.

iqtisad.f: Which two groups' positions on prophethood does al-Ghazālī reject?
iqtisad.b: He rejects the Muʿtazilah, who considered sending prophets obligatory upon God, and the Brahmins, who considered it impossible.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is sending prophets metaphysically possible?
iqtisad.b: Because God can speak by eternal inner speech, create signs expressing that speech, appoint a messenger, and support him with miracles. None of these involve any contradiction.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what constitutes the sending of a messenger?
iqtisad.b: It consists of God's eternal speech concerning beneficial and harmful matters, His appointing a person to convey it, and His supporting that person with a miracle confirming his claim.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why can objections based on divine wisdom or ugliness not invalidate prophethood?
iqtisad.b: Because he has already argued that judgments of beauty and ugliness do not impose obligations upon God.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the Brahmins' first objection against prophethood?
iqtisad.b: If prophets teach only what reason already knows, they are unnecessary; if they teach what contradicts reason, they cannot be believed.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the claim that prophets are unnecessary because reason is sufficient?
iqtisad.b: He says prophets chiefly inform people of matters that reason cannot discover independently—such as what leads to salvation or destruction in the Hereafter—although reason can understand and verify these teachings once they are revealed.

iqtisad.f: What analogy does al-Ghazālī use to explain why revelation complements rather than replaces reason?
iqtisad.b: He compares revelation to a physician's guidance about medicines: reason cannot independently discover the healing properties of drugs, but once informed, it can understand and benefit from the physician's advice.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why can miracles such as reviving the dead or splitting the sea not be equated with magic?
iqtisad.b: Al-Ghazālī argues that no rational person considers magic capable of producing miracles such as reviving the dead, turning a staff into a serpent, splitting the moon, parting the sea, or healing the blind and leprous. If someone claims that every act within God's power can be produced by magic, that claim is self-evidently false. If they admit a distinction, then miracles can be recognized as belonging to a different category from magic.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, when should a claimed miracle be accepted as genuine rather than magic?
iqtisad.b: If there is doubt whether an extraordinary event is magic or a miracle, it should not be accepted until the claimant publicly challenges the greatest magicians, grants them sufficient opportunity to respond, and they fail to produce anything comparable.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī not discuss individual miracles in this section?
iqtisad.b: Because his purpose is to establish the principle that miracles are distinguishable from magic, not to investigate particular miracles individually.

iqtisad.f: What is the third objection to prophethood that al-Ghazālī addresses?
iqtisad.b: The objection claims that even if miracles are distinguished from magic, one still cannot know that God intends guidance rather than deception. Perhaps God wishes to mislead people through the prophet by presenting what is actually harmful as beneficial and vice versa.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain that a miracle proves a prophet's truthfulness?
iqtisad.b: He argues that once one understands the meaning of prophethood and how miracles function as evidence, it becomes clear that deception is excluded. A miracle serves as God's authentication of the prophet.

iqtisad.f: What analogy does al-Ghazālī use to explain how a miracle authenticates a prophet?
iqtisad.b: He compares it to a man claiming before a king's army that he is the king's messenger. If the king responds to the claimant's request by performing a previously agreed extraordinary action, everyone necessarily knows that the king has confirmed and appointed him as his messenger.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is a miracle equivalent to God's saying, "You are My messenger"?
iqtisad.b: Because the miracle is God's own extraordinary action performed in direct response to the claimant's challenge, functioning as an act of appointment and confirmation rather than merely conveying information.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say that appointment through a miracle cannot involve falsehood?
iqtisad.b: Because falsehood applies to reports, whereas appointing someone as a messenger is an act of authorization and delegation, not a statement that could be true or false.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what have people historically denied about prophets instead of claiming that God authenticated false messengers?
iqtisad.b: They denied either that the prophets' wonders were genuine miracles, attributing them instead to magic or deception, or they denied the existence of a speaking God who sends and authenticates messengers.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what knowledge necessarily follows once someone accepts that a miracle is God's act?
iqtisad.b: Once a person accepts that the miracle is truly God's act accompanying a claim to prophethood, they necessarily know that the claimant is truthful.

iqtisad.f: What further objection does al-Ghazālī answer regarding God's direct speech?
iqtisad.b: The objection asks how people could trust even hearing God directly say, "This is My messenger," since perhaps God intended to deceive people by presenting what leads to ruin as salvation.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the claim that God might deceive by speaking falsely?
iqtisad.b: He replies that falsehood is impossible in God's eternal speech because God's speech is not composed of sounds or letters but is an eternal meaning subsisting in His essence, and such internal speech necessarily conforms to knowledge.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say falsehood is impossible in God's eternal speech?
iqtisad.b: Because eternal divine speech is an internal meaning corresponding perfectly to God's knowledge, and knowledge cannot contradict itself; therefore falsehood cannot arise in it.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, after what point is there no room for doubt about a prophet's truthfulness?
iqtisad.b: Once it is known that the extraordinary act is truly God's act and beyond human power, with the prophet claiming prophethood, certainty of the prophet's truthfulness necessarily follows.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, where can doubt about miracles legitimately remain?
iqtisad.b: Doubt may remain only over whether the extraordinary event was truly beyond human capability or whether it could have been produced by human means such as magic.

iqtisad.f: What is al-Ghazālī's position on the possibility of saints' miracles (karāmāt)?
iqtisad.b: He holds that karāmāt are genuinely possible because they consist of God breaking customary patterns in response to a saint's supplication or need, and nothing about this is intrinsically impossible.

iqtisad.f: Why do karāmāt not invalidate prophetic miracles according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Because a karāmah occurs without a claim to prophethood or public challenge, whereas a miracle is accompanied by a prophetic challenge and therefore serves as proof of prophethood.

iqtisad.f: Can extraordinary events occur through a sinful person according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Yes. Since such extraordinary acts are within God's power, He may produce them even through a sinful person, provided they are not accompanied by a claim to prophethood.

iqtisad.f: Can God produce a miracle on behalf of a liar according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: No. A miracle accompanying a claim to prophethood is equivalent to God declaring, "You are My messenger." Authenticating a liar in this way is intrinsically impossible because the very authentication would make him a true messenger rather than a liar.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī conclude that producing a miracle for a false prophet is impossible?
iqtisad.b: Because it combines two contradictory realities: the claimant being a liar and God simultaneously appointing him as His messenger. Since this is a logical contradiction, it is impossible, and impossibilities are not objects of divine power.

iqtisad.f: What is the purpose of the fourth section (al-qutb al-rābiʿ) of al-Ghazālī’s al-Iqtiṣād fī al-Iʿtiqād?
iqtisad.b: The purpose of the fourth section is to establish the prophethood of Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ and to prove the truth of the matters he conveyed, such as the resurrection and other unseen matters.

iqtisad.f: What are the four chapters included in al-Ghazālī’s fourth section on prophethood?
iqtisad.b: The four chapters are: (1) establishing the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ, (2) proving the truth of resurrection, gathering, the bridge, the scale, and punishment of the grave, (3) examining three specific issues, and (4) explaining which groups must be declared unbelievers and the principles governing takfīr.

iqtisad.f: Which group claimed that Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ was only sent to the Arabs and not to other peoples?
iqtisad.b: The ʿĪsawiyyah claimed that Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ was a true messenger but was sent only to the Arabs.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that the ʿĪsawiyyah’s restriction of Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ’s ﷺ mission to Arabs is impossible?
iqtisad.b: Because they already accepted that Muḥammad ﷺ was a true messenger, and a true messenger cannot lie. Since he claimed to be sent to all humans and jinn and sent messages to rulers such as Caesar and Chosroes, their claim contradicts his truthful statement.

iqtisad.f: Which group rejected Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ because they believed no prophet could come after Moses عليه السلام?
iqtisad.b: The Jews rejected Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ based on their belief that there could be no prophet after Moses عليه السلام.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why should the prophethood of Jesus عليه السلام be established first when debating Jews?
iqtisad.b: Because Jews may not recognize the miraculous nature of the Qur’an, but they can understand physical miracles such as reviving the dead and healing the blind and the leper.

iqtisad.f: What comparison does al-Ghazālī use to challenge those who accept some miracles but reject others?
iqtisad.b: He asks why someone would accept a miracle such as reviving the dead as proof of truth but reject turning a staff into a serpent as proof, since both are extraordinary signs beyond normal human ability.

iqtisad.f: What two objections did Jews raise against prophets coming after Moses عليه السلام?
iqtisad.b: They argued: (1) abrogation (naskh) is impossible because it implies change in God, and (2) Moses عليه السلام supposedly declared that his law would remain forever and that no prophet would come after him.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī define abrogation (naskh) in Islamic law?
iqtisad.b: Abrogation is a later command from God indicating the removal of a previous ruling that was understood to continue, even though its duration was known to God from the beginning.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say abrogation does not imply that God changes His knowledge?
iqtisad.b: Because God may know from the beginning that a ruling is beneficial only for a certain period, while not revealing that period to His servants. Changing the ruling later does not mean He learned something new.

iqtisad.f: What example does al-Ghazālī give to explain why a command can later be changed without implying ignorance?
iqtisad.b: He gives the example of a master telling his servant, “Stand,” without mentioning a time limit. The master may already know when standing will stop being beneficial, but he later commands him to sit when that time arrives.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, does the arrival of a new prophet automatically cancel all previous revealed laws?
iqtisad.b: No. A new prophet does not cancel previous laws merely by arriving, nor does he cancel most rulings. Only certain rulings change according to different circumstances and benefits.

iqtisad.f: What examples of legal changes between prophets does al-Ghazālī mention?
iqtisad.b: He mentions changes such as the alteration of the direction of prayer and making certain previously prohibited matters permissible.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say changes in religious rulings do not indicate contradiction in God’s law?
iqtisad.b: Because rulings may differ according to different times, circumstances, and benefits. A change reflects wisdom in different situations, not a change in God’s knowledge.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that denying all prophets after Moses عليه السلام would also require denying earlier prophets?
iqtisad.b: Because if Moses عليه السلام’ law being final meant no other prophetic laws could exist, then prophets before Moses عليه السلام, such as Noah عليه السلام and Abraham عليه السلام, would also have to be rejected, even though their existence and laws are known through mass transmission.

iqtisad.f: What argument does al-Ghazālī give against the claim that Moses عليه السلام declared himself the final prophet?
iqtisad.b: He argues that if Moses عليه السلام had truly made such a declaration, Jews would have used it as their strongest argument against Islam, especially when they were eager to criticize Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ and defend their religion.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say the Jews’ failure to use Moses عليه السلام’ alleged statement proves it was not authentic?
iqtisad.b: Because such a decisive argument would have been impossible for them to abandon. They searched for every possible criticism against Islam, so they would certainly have transmitted and used such a statement if it existed.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī argue that Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ affirmed Moses عليه السلام’ law rather than rejecting it?
iqtisad.b: He points out that Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ believed in Moses عليه السلام and even judged the Jews according to their own Torah in matters such as the punishment of stoning.

iqtisad.f: What conclusion does al-Ghazālī reach after responding to the Jewish objections?
iqtisad.b: He concludes that once the prophethood of Jesus عليه السلام is established, the same principles can be used to establish the prophethood of Muḥammad ﷺ.

iqtisad.f: Which third group rejected the prophethood of Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: The third group accepted the possibility of abrogation (naskh) but rejected the prophethood of Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ because they denied the miraculous nature of the Qur’an.

iqtisad.f: How many methods does al-Ghazālī mention for proving the prophethood of Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ through miracles?
iqtisad.b: Al-Ghazālī mentions two methods: (1) proving his prophethood through the miracle of the Qur’an, and (2) proving it through the collection of other extraordinary events that occurred through him.

iqtisad.f: What is the first method al-Ghazālī uses to prove the prophethood of Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ?
iqtisad.b: The first method is to establish the miraculous nature of the Qur’an and show that it was an unmatched challenge which the Arabs were unable to answer.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī define a miracle (muʿjizah)?
iqtisad.b: A miracle is an extraordinary event accompanied by a prophet’s challenge, presented as evidence of his truthfulness, in a manner that humans are unable to reproduce or oppose.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī argue that the Qur’anic challenge to the Arabs is established with certainty?
iqtisad.b: Because Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ openly challenged the Arabs with the Qur’an, the Arabs were known for their extreme mastery of eloquence, and their failure to produce a rival composition is well established.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say that the Arabs’ inability to oppose the Qur’an cannot be denied?
iqtisad.b: Because if they had been capable of producing something comparable, they would have done so, since opposing the Qur’an would have been far easier than fighting wars against Muslims and would have protected their religion, wealth, and lives.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say that if the Arabs had produced a rival to the Qur’an it would have been transmitted?
iqtisad.b: Because even ordinary poets’ works and their disputes were preserved and transmitted. Therefore, a successful response to the Qur’an would certainly have become famous.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī use the Qur’anic miracle to establish the prophethood of Jesus عليه السلام by analogy?
iqtisad.b: He argues that the same reasoning applies to Jesus عليه السلام: opponents cannot deny his challenge, his miracles such as reviving the dead, the occurrence of those miracles, or the absence of successful opposition without contradicting established historical realities.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī identify as the miraculous aspects of the Qur’an?
iqtisad.b: He identifies the combination of extraordinary eloquence (faṣāḥah), powerful expression (jazālah), and a unique structure and style unlike the speech forms of Arabs in poetry, sermons, and other genres.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say that merely copying the Qur’an’s style does not produce an equal work?
iqtisad.b: Because someone may imitate its structure after learning from it, but they cannot combine that structure with the same level of eloquence. Their attempts remain weak and are ridiculed by experts in Arabic.

iqtisad.f: What example does al-Ghazālī give of a failed attempt to imitate Qur’anic style?
iqtisad.b: He mentions the statements attributed to Musaylimah the Liar, such as: “The elephant, and what do you know of the elephant? It has a thick tail and a long trunk,” which imitate form but lack eloquence.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say the Arabs’ reaction proves the Qur’an’s miraculous eloquence?
iqtisad.b: Because the Arabs, who were the greatest experts in eloquence, were astonished by the Qur’an, and no credible report exists of any Arab master of language successfully criticizing its eloquence or matching it.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the claim that the Arabs did not challenge the Qur’an because they were busy fighting Muslims?
iqtisad.b: He argues that this is unreasonable because producing a rival speech would have been much easier than fighting wars, suffering death, captivity, and loss of wealth.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is the Arabs’ turning away from challenging the Qur’an itself a miracle?
iqtisad.b: Because their inability or lack of motivation to perform the challenge, despite their urgent need to disprove the Prophet ﷺ, indicates a divine prevention (ṣarf) from opposing it.

iqtisad.f: What example does al-Ghazālī give to explain that preventing opposition can itself be miraculous?
iqtisad.b: He says that if a prophet claimed, “My sign is that I will move my finger today and no human will be able to oppose me,” and nobody could move their fingers despite having healthy limbs, that inability would itself be a miracle.

iqtisad.f: What is the second method al-Ghazālī uses to prove Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ’s ﷺ prophethood?
iqtisad.b: The second method is proving his prophethood through the numerous extraordinary events that occurred through him, such as the splitting of the moon, animals speaking, water flowing from his fingers, stones glorifying God in his hand, and multiplication of small amounts of food.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the objection that individual miracles of Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ were not transmitted through mass transmission (tawātur)?
iqtisad.b: He argues that even if individual reports do not each reach tawātur, the total collection of many independent reports can reach certainty, just as a person’s bravery or generosity can become certain from many individual reports.

iqtisad.f: What analogy does al-Ghazālī give for certainty arising from many individual reports?
iqtisad.b: He compares it to knowing the bravery of ʿAlī رضي الله عنه and the generosity of Ḥātim through many separate accounts, even though each individual event is not necessarily transmitted by tawātur.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to someone who claims that the miracles of Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ have not reached him through tawātur?
iqtisad.b: He says such a person should mix with the people among whom these reports are widespread. Someone who isolates himself, like a deaf person or someone pretending to be deaf, cannot expect reports to reach him.

iqtisad.f: What is the subject of the second chapter of the fourth section of al-Ghazālī’s al-Iqtiṣād?
iqtisad.b: It discusses the obligation to affirm matters reported by revelation which reason considers possible.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, into how many categories are non-obvious matters divided?
iqtisad.b: They are divided into three categories: matters known through reason alone, matters known through revelation alone, and matters known through both reason and revelation.

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī give of matters known through reason alone?
iqtisad.b: He gives the creation of the universe, the existence of its Creator, God’s power, knowledge, and will.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say these matters must be established before revelation can be accepted?
iqtisad.b: Because revelation depends upon proving God’s speech and existence. Without first establishing the Creator, His attributes, and His ability to communicate revelation, the foundation of religion cannot be established.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say that God’s eternal speech cannot itself be proven through revelation?
iqtisad.b: Because revelation depends upon God's speech being established first. Something that is logically prior to revelation cannot be proven by revelation itself.

iqtisad.f: What are the three categories into which things known by revelation (samʿ) and reason are divided?
iqtisad.b: Things not known by necessity are divided into: (1) what is known by rational proof alone, (2) what is known by revelation alone, and (3) what is known by both reason and revelation.

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī give of matters known by reason alone?
iqtisad.b: The origination of the world, the existence of its Creator, His power, knowledge, and will are known by reason alone, because revelation cannot be established until God's speech is established.

iqtisad.f: Why cannot the existence of God's speech be proven through revelation itself according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Because revelation depends upon God's speech, so anything that is prior in rank to God's speech cannot be proven through God's speech itself.

iqtisad.f: What type of knowledge is knowing that one possible thing was specifically chosen to occur rather than another?
iqtisad.b: It is known only through revelation, because reason recognizes possibilities but cannot know which possibility God chose to bring into existence.

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī give of matters known through revelation alone?
iqtisad.b: Resurrection, gathering of creation, reward, punishment, and other matters known through revelation from God.

iqtisad.f: What matters does al-Ghazālī say are known through both reason and revelation?
iqtisad.b: Matters that are possible according to reason and occur after establishing God's speech, such as seeing Allah (ruʾyah), Allah alone creating movements, and similar theological issues.

iqtisad.f: What is the rule when revelation brings something that reason permits?
iqtisad.b: It must be believed if the revealed evidence is decisive in both wording and transmission; it should be believed with probability if the evidence is only probable.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say that probable evidence can establish belief-related matters just as it can establish practical matters?
iqtisad.b: Because acceptance of a belief through the tongue and heart is an action, and actions can be based upon probable evidence like legal rulings.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain that the Companions used general texts as evidence against the belief that humans create their own actions?
iqtisad.b: They rejected the claim based on the verse “Allah is the Creator of everything,” even though its general wording could theoretically allow exceptions; the issue became certain after rational investigation.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī say about revelation containing something that reason proves impossible?
iqtisad.b: Such revelation must be interpreted figuratively, because decisive revelation cannot contradict decisive reason.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to anthropomorphic (tashbīh) narrations?
iqtisad.b: He says most narrations suggesting resemblance are not authentic, and the authentic ones are not decisive and can be interpreted.

iqtisad.f: What is required for accepting a revealed matter that reason neither proves possible nor impossible?
iqtisad.b: It is enough that reason does not judge it impossible; one must accept it due to the revealed evidence.

iqtisad.f: What distinction does al-Ghazālī make between knowing something is possible and merely not knowing whether it is possible or impossible?
iqtisad.b: Knowing something is possible is positive knowledge, while merely lacking knowledge of its impossibility is ignorance of its status; these are vastly different.

iqtisad.f: Is knowledge that something is possible required for believing revelation according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: No. It is enough that reason does not judge it impossible.

iqtisad.f: What is the subject of the first chapter of the second section of the fourth pole?
iqtisad.b: The rational justification of what revelation has brought regarding resurrection, gathering, punishment in the grave, the bridge (ṣirāṭ), and the scale (mīzān).

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī mean by resurrection (ḥashr)?
iqtisad.b: He means the restoration and gathering of creation after death.

iqtisad.f: What proof does al-Ghazālī give for the possibility of resurrection?
iqtisad.b: He argues from the possibility of initial creation: the One capable of creating something the first time is capable of recreating it.

iqtisad.f: Which Qurʾānic meaning does al-Ghazālī mention as evidence for resurrection?
iqtisad.b: The meaning of the verse: “Say: He will bring them to life who created them the first time.”

iqtisad.f: Does al-Ghazālī claim that revelation decisively determines whether bodies and accidents are both destroyed and recreated?
iqtisad.b: No. He says revelation does not decisively specify one of these possibilities.

iqtisad.f: What are the two possibilities al-Ghazālī mentions regarding what happens to the human body before resurrection?
iqtisad.b: Either the accidents disappear while the body remains in some form, or the entire body is destroyed and recreated again.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, why is recreating accidents possible despite some scholars denying it?
iqtisad.b: Because accidents do not persist according to his theological view; life, color, and other qualities are continuously recreated, so there is no impossibility in recreating them.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what makes a resurrected person the same person rather than merely a similar person?
iqtisad.b: It is based on God's knowledge distinguishing between what previously existed and what never existed, not merely physical continuity.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain the difference between "recreation" (iʿādah) and "creating a likeness" (mithl)?
iqtisad.b: Recreation applies to bringing into existence what God previously knew would exist; creating a likeness applies to creating something that had no previous existence.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī avoid discussing the exact nature of the soul and spirit in this discussion?
iqtisad.b: Because investigating the realities of the soul, spirit, and life would lead into deeper philosophical questions beyond what is needed for basic creed.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī say about punishment in the grave?
iqtisad.b: He says it is established by decisive revelation and must be believed because it is possible according to reason.

iqtisad.f: What evidences does al-Ghazālī mention for punishment in the grave?
iqtisad.b: The Prophet ﷺ and the Companions frequently seeking refuge from it in supplications, the report about the two graves whose inhabitants were being punished, and the verse concerning Pharaoh’s people being exposed to the Fire morning and evening.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the objection that people do not see the dead being punished?
iqtisad.b: He considers this objection invalid because unseen matters cannot be judged by ordinary physical observation, and the objection does not establish impossibility.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the objection that people see the dead body but do not see punishment in the grave?
iqtisad.b: He says that seeing a person only means seeing the outward body, while the perception of punishment belongs to an inner part of the human being, such as the heart or inward faculty.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say bodily stillness does not prove the absence of pain or pleasure?
iqtisad.b: Because pain and pleasure are not necessarily manifested through outward bodily movements.

iqtisad.f: What example does al-Ghazālī give to show that someone may experience things unseen by observers?
iqtisad.b: He gives the example of a sleeping person who experiences pleasure in dreams or pain when imagining being struck, while an observer sees only a motionless body.

iqtisad.f: How would someone unfamiliar with sleep react if a sleeping person described their experiences after waking?
iqtisad.b: They would likely deny them because they were deceived by seeing the body remain still.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain the case of animals eating the dead body?
iqtisad.b: He says that the stomach of the animal may function as the grave, and God can restore life to a part capable of perceiving punishment.

iqtisad.f: Does a person need to feel pain throughout the entire body in order to be punished?
iqtisad.b: No. Al-Ghazālī says a person may experience pain through only a particular part that perceives it.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī say about the questioning by Munkar and Nakīr?
iqtisad.b: He says it is true, established by revelation, and must be believed because it is possible according to reason.

iqtisad.f: What does the questioning of Munkar and Nakīr require according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: It requires only that they communicate a question and that the deceased understand and respond.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī say is required for understanding and answering the angels’ questions?
iqtisad.b: It requires life in a part capable of understanding and responding.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say that a part of the human being being given life is possible?
iqtisad.b: Because human understanding does not occur through the entire body but through an inward part, and Allah is capable of bringing life to that part.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the objection: “We see the dead person but do not see Munkar and Nakīr or hear their voices”?
iqtisad.b: He compares it to revelation: the Prophet ﷺ saw and heard Jibrīl while those around him, including ʿĀʾishah رضي الله عنها, did not see or hear him.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say denying the unseen experiences of the grave leads to a problematic conclusion?
iqtisad.b: Because it would require denying other established experiences, such as the Prophet’s ﷺ seeing Jibrīl and the experiences of sleepers.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain why others did not see Jibrīl when the Prophet ﷺ saw him?
iqtisad.b: Allah created the Prophet ﷺ with the ability to see and hear Jibrīl but did not create that perception in those around him.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī say about denying these matters due to lack of ordinary observation?
iqtisad.b: He says such denial comes from rejecting the vastness of Allah’s power.

iqtisad.f: What comparison does al-Ghazālī make between denying punishment in the grave and denying human creation from a drop of fluid?
iqtisad.b: He says both are rejected by some people because of unfamiliarity and imagination, yet the creation of humans from a lowly substance itself contains greater wonders.

iqtisad.f: What principle does al-Ghazālī establish regarding things that are not proven impossible?
iqtisad.b: He says that anything which has no proof of impossibility should not be rejected merely because it seems unlikely or strange.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī say about the Scale (Mīzān)?
iqtisad.b: He says the Scale is true, established by decisive revelation, and must be believed because it is possible.

iqtisad.f: What objection does al-Ghazālī mention regarding weighing deeds?
iqtisad.b: The objection is that deeds are accidents, accidents disappear, and something nonexistent cannot be weighed.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī answer the objection that deeds cannot be weighed because they are not physical objects?
iqtisad.b: He says the Prophet ﷺ explained that the records of deeds (ṣuḥuf) are weighed, and Allah creates in the scale the appropriate weight corresponding to the rank of the deeds.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is weighed according to the Prophetic explanation?
iqtisad.b: The records containing the deeds written by the noble recording angels are weighed.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain how the weight of deeds corresponds to their value?
iqtisad.b: Allah creates a weight in the scale proportional to the rank and value of the deeds, according to His power.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī say when asked about the purpose of the Scale?
iqtisad.b: He says one should not demand a purpose for Allah’s actions because “He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned.”

iqtisad.f: What possible benefit does al-Ghazālī mention for the Scale if someone insists on seeking wisdom behind it?
iqtisad.b: The servant may witness the measure of his deeds and know that Allah’s judgment is either justice or gracious forgiveness.

iqtisad.f: What analogy does al-Ghazālī give to explain why Allah may show a person the measure of their deeds?
iqtisad.b: He compares it to a person who intends to punish or forgive an agent for wrongdoing and first shows him the extent of his wrongdoing so that justice or pardon is understood.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī say about the Ṣirāṭ (bridge over Hell)?
iqtisad.b: He says it is true, established by revelation, and must be believed because it is possible.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī define the Ṣirāṭ?
iqtisad.b: It is a bridge stretched over Hell which all creation will approach and cross.

iqtisad.f: What question is raised about the Ṣirāṭ being narrower than a hair and sharper than a sword?
iqtisad.b: The objection asks how anyone could possibly walk across such a bridge.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to someone who rejects the possibility of crossing the Ṣirāṭ?
iqtisad.b: If they deny Allah’s power, the discussion returns to proving His unlimited power; if they accept His power, walking on such a bridge is no more impossible than walking in the air.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say walking on the Ṣirāṭ is not more difficult than walking in the air?
iqtisad.b: Because Allah can create in a person the ability to walk without falling and can prevent the air from causing them to descend.

iqtisad.f: What conclusion does al-Ghazālī draw from the possibility of walking in the air?
iqtisad.b: Since walking in the air is within Allah’s power, the Ṣirāṭ is even more clearly possible.

iqtisad.f: What is the purpose of al-Ghazālī’s second chapter in the fourth pole?
iqtisad.b: It explains why he omitted certain theological discussions from his concise creed, because brief creeds should only contain what is necessary for sound belief.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī avoid including every theological discussion in a creed?
iqtisad.b: Because many issues do not need to be brought to mind, and ignorance of them does not constitute sin; discussing them is investigation into realities beyond what is needed for correcting belief.

iqtisad.f: What three types of sciences contain the issues al-Ghazālī omitted from his creed?
iqtisad.b: They are: rational sciences, linguistic/verbal sciences, and jurisprudential sciences.

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī give of omitted rational theological discussions?
iqtisad.b: Questions such as whether created power relates to opposites simultaneously, whether it relates to different things, and whether created power can relate to an action occurring outside its location.

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī give of omitted linguistic theological discussions?
iqtisad.b: Questions such as the exact meaning of provision (rizq), the limits of guidance (tawfīq), abandonment (khidhlān), and faith (īmān).

iqtisad.f: What examples does al-Ghazālī give of omitted jurisprudential discussions?
iqtisad.b: Questions such as when commanding the good becomes obligatory and what the ruling of repentance is.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what are the truly important foundations of belief?
iqtisad.b: Belief in Allah’s essence, His attributes and their implications, His actions being possible rather than obligatory upon Him, and the truthfulness of the Prophet ﷺ and everything he conveyed.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say that matters beyond these foundations are not essential?
iqtisad.b: Because they do not affect the validity of a person's basic creed.

iqtisad.f: What example does al-Ghazālī give from the rational discussions he omitted?
iqtisad.b: The question of whether someone who is killed died by his appointed lifespan (ajal), and whether he would have died at the same time if he had not been killed.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī begin analyzing whether killing and death are connected?
iqtisad.b: He first explains the general relationship between two things that occur together.

iqtisad.f: If two things occur together but have no connection, does removing one require removing the other?
iqtisad.b: No. The removal of one does not necessarily imply the removal of the other.

iqtisad.f: What example does al-Ghazālī give of two things occurring together without a necessary connection?
iqtisad.b: If Zayd and ʿAmr both die, imagining Zayd not dying does not necessarily mean that ʿAmr would not die.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain the relationship between death and an eclipse?
iqtisad.b: If someone dies during an eclipse, removing the death does not require removing the eclipse, nor does removing the eclipse require removing the death.

iqtisad.f: How many categories of relationships between things does al-Ghazālī mention?
iqtisad.b: Three categories: reciprocal relationships, condition and conditioned relationships, and cause-and-effect relationships.

iqtisad.f: What is the first category of relationship according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: A reciprocal relationship where each thing depends on the other for its meaning, such as right and left or above and below.

iqtisad.f: Why does removing one thing in a reciprocal relationship require removing the other?
iqtisad.b: Because neither side can be understood or exist as a relational concept without the other.

iqtisad.f: What is the second category of relationship according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: A relationship where one thing is a condition for another but they are not reciprocal, such as life being a condition for knowledge.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī describe a condition (sharṭ)?
iqtisad.b: It is something necessary for the existence of another thing, but the thing does not exist because of it as a cause; rather, it exists through it and alongside it.

iqtisad.f: What example does al-Ghazālī give of a condition relationship?
iqtisad.b: A person’s life is a condition for knowledge, and knowledge is a condition for will; removing life removes knowledge, and removing knowledge removes will.

iqtisad.f: What is the third category of relationship according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: The relationship between a cause and its effect.

iqtisad.f: Does removing one cause always remove an effect?
iqtisad.b: Only if the effect has no other possible cause; otherwise, removing one cause does not necessarily remove the effect.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī apply these principles to killing and death?
iqtisad.b: He examines whether the cutting of the neck is actually connected to death as a cause, or whether both are simply created together by Allah.

iqtisad.f: What does killing consist of according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: It consists of movements in the hand of the killer and sword, and separations occurring in the parts of the victim’s neck.

iqtisad.f: According to the Ashʿarī view described by al-Ghazālī, is killing the true cause of death?
iqtisad.b: No. Death is independently created by Allah, and killing is merely something that occurs alongside it.

iqtisad.f: According to the Ashʿarī position, if killing did not occur, would death necessarily not occur?
iqtisad.b: No. Since Allah creates death independently, death could occur through another circumstance or without the killing.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say this is the correct view according to Ahl al-Sunnah?
iqtisad.b: Because they believe Allah alone originates all events and created things do not generate other created things.

iqtisad.f: How does someone who believes in natural causation understand death?
iqtisad.b: They believe death has natural causes, and that every body has a natural lifespan determined by its constitution unless an external factor cuts it short.

iqtisad.f: According to the natural causation view, what does “lifespan” (ajal) mean?
iqtisad.b: It means the natural duration a thing would continue according to its own nature if left uninterrupted.

iqtisad.f: What analogy does al-Ghazālī give for the natural causation understanding of lifespan?
iqtisad.b: He compares it to a wall that naturally lasts one hundred years due to its construction but can be destroyed immediately with an axe.

iqtisad.f: According to the natural causation view, would someone killed by an axe be considered to have died at their appointed lifespan?
iqtisad.b: No, because the axe shortened their natural lifespan.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī’s Ashʿarī view, why should a person who is killed still be said to have died at his appointed time?
iqtisad.b: Because the appointed lifespan is the time Allah created that person’s death, whether accompanied by killing, an eclipse, rain, or nothing observable.

iqtisad.f: According to al-Ghazālī, what is the role of events such as killing, eclipses, and rain in relation to death?
iqtisad.b: They are accompanying circumstances, not independent causes; some repeatedly accompany events through habit while others do not.

iqtisad.f: What does al-Ghazālī say about the source of disagreement in this issue?
iqtisad.b: He says many people debate the matter without recognizing that the real issue is the doctrine of divine power and whether created things generate effects.

iqtisad.f: What theological principle does this discussion depend upon according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: It depends on affirming Allah’s unrestricted power and rejecting the idea that created things produce effects independently (tawallud).

iqtisad.f: What is the source of disagreement regarding whether īmān increases and decreases according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: The disagreement originates from ignorance that the word īmān is a shared term (mushtarak) used for different meanings. Once the meanings intended by the word are separated, the disagreement disappears.

iqtisad.f: What are the three meanings in which the term īmān is used according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: The term īmān may refer to: (1) certain rationally demonstrated conviction (taṣdīq yaqīnī burhānī), (2) firmly held traditional belief (taṣdīq taqlīdī with certainty), and (3) conviction accompanied by acting according to its requirements.

iqtisad.f: Why is the first meaning of īmān, namely rationally demonstrated certainty, not subject to increase or decrease?
iqtisad.b: Because complete certainty has no level beyond it. If certainty exists fully, it cannot increase; and if it does not exist fully, then it is not true certainty.

iqtisad.f: How can certainty appear to increase despite certainty itself not increasing?
iqtisad.b: The increase may refer to the tranquility of the soul (ṭumaʾnīnah) toward the certainty. A person may have certainty initially, then become more reassured as more proofs accumulate.

iqtisad.f: What example does al-Ghazālī give to show differences in levels of inner reassurance?
iqtisad.b: He says people perceive a difference between their certainty that two is greater than one and their certainty that the universe has a Creator. Likewise, some beliefs become more firmly settled through possessing more proofs.

iqtisad.f: Can īmān increase or decrease when it means traditional conviction (īmān taqlīdī)?
iqtisad.b: Yes. There is observable variation in the strength of traditional beliefs. Two people may both hold firm beliefs, yet one person's conviction may be more deeply rooted and resistant to doubts than another's.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī explain the difference in strength between different people's traditional beliefs?
iqtisad.b: He compares belief in the heart to a knot: the knot differs in strength and weakness. Some people's beliefs are deeply rooted and their hearts are not easily affected by doubts, while others are less firmly established.

iqtisad.f: Why do some people deny differences in the strength of beliefs according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Because they only know the names of concepts from books and have not experienced the realities of belief within themselves or observed differences in their own spiritual states.

iqtisad.f: When īmān means belief together with action, is increase and decrease obvious?
iqtisad.b: Yes. Since actions themselves increase and decrease, īmān in this sense clearly varies according to the amount of deeds performed.

iqtisad.f: Does performing acts of obedience increase the strength of conviction itself according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Yes. Continuous obedience strengthens the soul's tranquility toward its beliefs and makes those beliefs more firmly established.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī illustrate the effect of actions upon belief?
iqtisad.b: He compares it to someone who believes in mercy toward an orphan: when he acts upon that mercy by caring for the orphan, his feeling of mercy becomes stronger. Likewise, humility increases when a person performs acts of humility.

iqtisad.f: Why were acts such as bowing and prostration prescribed according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: Because outward actions corresponding to reverence strengthen the inner state of reverence in the heart.

iqtisad.f: What criticism does al-Ghazālī make of some theologians who reject this effect of actions?
iqtisad.b: He criticizes those who only understand theoretical definitions from words but have not experienced the realities of spiritual states through observation of their own souls.

iqtisad.f: What other disagreement does al-Ghazālī say arises from confusion over meanings of words?
iqtisad.b: The disagreement regarding the meaning of rizq (provision) arises from the same issue of unclear terminology.

iqtisad.f: How do the Muʿtazilah define rizq according to al-Ghazālī?
iqtisad.b: They restrict rizq to what a person owns, which would imply that Allah does not provide animals with sustenance.

iqtisad.f: How do al-Ghazālī and his Ashʿarī companions define rizq?
iqtisad.b: They define rizq as anything from which benefit is received, whether it is lawful or unlawful.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī criticize lengthy discussions about definitions such as rizq and niʿmah?
iqtisad.b: Because they are not among the important matters of religion, and spending one's limited lifespan on such debates wastes time that should be devoted to more important concerns.

iqtisad.f: What third example does al-Ghazālī give of unnecessary theological debate?
iqtisad.b: The question of whether a sinful person (fāsiq) may perform ḥisbah (commanding good and forbidding evil).

iqtisad.f: What is al-Ghazālī's position on whether a sinful person may perform ḥisbah?
iqtisad.b: He holds that a sinful person may perform ḥisbah.

iqtisad.f: Why cannot being completely free from sins be a condition for performing ḥisbah?
iqtisad.b: Because that would contradict consensus, since even the protection of prophets from sins is known through revelation, and scholars differed regarding minor sins. If complete sinlessness were required, almost no one could command good or forbid evil.

iqtisad.f: What example does al-Ghazālī give to show that sinners may command others to leave sins?
iqtisad.b: He says a person wearing silk (which is sinful for men according to the discussion) may still forbid others from adultery or drinking alcohol.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī reject the idea that a person cannot forbid a sin unless he avoids an equal or lesser sin himself?
iqtisad.b: Because there is no proof establishing this rule. A person may commit one sin while still being obligated to prevent another sin.

iqtisad.f: How does al-Ghazālī respond to the argument that someone who drinks alcohol cannot forbid others from drinking?
iqtisad.b: He says both avoiding alcohol and forbidding others from alcohol are separate obligations. Failing one obligation does not remove the duty of performing the other.

iqtisad.f: Why does al-Ghazālī say a sinner may even forbid greater sins than the one he commits?
iqtisad.b: Because obligations are independent. A person may fail in one duty while still being responsible for fulfilling another duty, such as preventing greater wrongdoing.

iqtisad.f: What general principle does al-Ghazālī highlight through these examples?
iqtisad.b: Many theological disputes arise from confusion over terminology or from discussing matters that are not essential to correct belief. The important matters are those necessary for sound faith.

iqtisad.f: What objection is raised against al-Ghazālī's view that a sinner may perform ḥisbah (commanding good and forbidding evil)?
iqtisad.b: The objection is that this leads to absurd consequences: for example, a man committing adultery by force could forbid the woman from uncovering her face, claiming that exposing her face to a non-maḥram is forbidden while ignoring his own greater sin.

iqtisad.f: How do the objectors describe the ḥisbah of a person committing a greater sin while forbidding a lesser sin?
